research.abstract: Centromeres are essential for chromosome function, yet how contrasting centromere architectures shape polyploid genome evolution and plant diversification remains unresolved. In monocentric chromosomes, centromeric activity is restricted to one chromosomal region; in holocentric chromosomes, it is distributed along the chromosome length. Hybridization followed by genome doubling can place chromosome sets with different centromeres, repeat complements, and rearrangement histories in the same nucleus. We examined whether such genomic mergers are associated with later chromosome restructuring in carnivorous Caryophyllales, focusing on chromosome-scale assemblies of putatively holocentric Drosera regia and monocentric D. capensis. The two sundews retain broad syntenic continuity and related polyploid ancestry, but their present genomes differ sharply. D. regia preserves several ancestral chromosomal fusions and dispersed candidate centromere-associated satellite repeats, whereas D. capensis has stronger internal duplication, extensive rearrangement, and localized centromeres. Phylogenomic and structural analyses suggest a reticulate evolutionary history for D. regia, with part of its genome showing preferential structural affinity to the Venus flytrap lineage. Whereas D. regia exhibits threefold syntenic depth consistent with hexaploidy, D. capensis exhibits sixfold depth consistent with dodecaploidy, and structural comparisons do not support simple doubling of the extant D. regia-like architecture. Repeat profiling across a broad sample of Drosera also shows rapid turnover and species-level differences in centromere-associated DNA. These results place centromere organization alongside polyploid history and chromosome restructuring as a major axis of genome evolution in sundews.

research.abstract: Bayesian phylogenetic inference produces large samples from a posterior distribution over phylogenetic trees that represents uncertainty in both tree topology and associated variables. Such a collection of trees is hard to interpret and it is common practice to summarize such samples into a single representative tree.Methods for constructing representative trees have largely been restricted to plain tree topologies, encoding only relationships among taxa. Inference with more sophisticated models produce annotated tree objects. These have additional information representing nodes' locations in the case of phylogeography, host information when inferring transmission trees, or sampled ancestor status when incorporating fossil information. Nevertheless, these annotated representations are reduced to a single representative tree, typically using methods developed for plain tree topologies and without accounting for the resulting methodological mismatch.Here, we introduce the concept of an extended clade and investigate an extension of the conditional clade distribution (CCD) model. Through motivating examples and case studies in discrete trait phylogeography and transmission tree reconstruction, we demonstrate limitations of standard summary tree approaches and show how these can be addressed using an extended CCD framework that explicitly incorporates the annotated tree structure.

research.abstract: Abstract All cellular life possesses environmental interfaces like cell membranes or cell walls, yet the compositional complexity of these major cell components limits structural and evolutionary studies. Prokaryotic surface layer (S-layer) exoskeletons, with their homopolymer paracrystalline architecture, offer a more tractable model of an environmental interface. However, extreme sequence diversity and heterogeneous multidomain organisation of S-layer proteins confound conventional evolutionary analyses. Here, by combining phylogenomics with structural modelling, we show that extensive sequence divergence, modular evolution and lateral gene transfer drive lineage-specific S-layer diversification across both monoderm ( Bacillaceae , Peptostreptococcaceae ) and diderm ( Caulobacteraceae , Deinococcaceae ) bacteria. Focusing on the Gram-positive order Peptostreptococcales , including environmental isolates and clinical pathogens, we uncover multiple S-layer architectures conferring divergent physiological properties. Molecular microbiology reveals that among close relatives utilising the same exoskeleton type, only pathogens display resistance to the antimicrobial immune effectors LL-37 and lysozyme. Furthermore, by experimentally determining two S-layer structures, we unravel how mechanisms including (intra)domain gains and losses generate hyper-diversity of homologous S-layers among clinical isolates of the pathogen Clostridioides difficile . Our findings establish the S-layer as a paradigm of molecular modularity and evolutionary plasticity. Specifically, evolution of a single structural protein enables rapid cell-surface reconfiguration and contributes to immune evasion in bacterial pathogens.

research.abstract: Forecasting the evolution of viral proteins can help inform pandemic preparedness and guide the development of interventions. Phylogenetic trees provide historical records of pathogen evolution, which are key for retrospective analysis, but using them to predict future genotypic changes remains challenging. We introduce antiGen, a machine learning model that learns from the evolutionary past of viruses to forecast the evolutionary future. antiGen achieves state-of-the-art performance in forecasting SARS-CoV-2 spike protein mutations according to a variety of metrics, including the prediction of mutations in the receptor binding domain, mutations never previously seen, and mutations with high prevalence. Most experimentally tested antiGen-forecasted spike variants retain pseudoviral infectivity in vitro, supporting their functional plausibility. Evaluations on surface proteins of influenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, and dengue virus further demonstrate applicability across viruses with differing amounts of available sequencing data. Finally, we develop a model trained across 49 viral proteins from 27 viruses, which improves forecasting performance over models trained on individual protein phylogenies. Together, these results support learning from phylogenetic histories as an approach to model viral amino acid changes prospectively, with applications in epidemiology and therapeutic development.

research.abstract: Estimating the effective sample size (ESS) is fundamental in Bayesian phylogenetic inference to account for autocorrelation in MCMC samples. While methods for continuous parameters are well established, the discrete and high-dimensional nature of treespace poses substantial challenges. In this paper, we introduce a new approach based on Conditional Clade Distributions (CCDs) to emulate MCMC chains with known ESS bounds. We compare existing tree ESS estimators with novel approaches that utilize CCDs as tractable tree distributions, as well as a new probabilistic estimator based on differences in clade frequencies between independent chains. Using our emulated chains from both simulated and real datasets, we assess estimators for their ability to recover the true ESS (accuracy), their insensitivity to the removal of autocorrelated samples from the chain (stability), and their tolerance to combining multiple chains together (robustness). We further examine how multimodality and poor inter-mode chain mixing can compromise the reliability of tree ESS estimates. These findings indicate that our new CCD-based estimators perform comparably to existing approaches with respect to accuracy, stability, and robustness. In contrast, the probabilistic estimator and two previously recommended methods incur prohibitive computational costs for long chains. Together, these results establish a new framework for evaluating tree ESS estimators using CCD-based emulated MCMC chains and demonstrate their performance and current limitations in practical phylogenetic analyses. The expanded suite of tree ESS estimators is available in the user-friendly TreeStat2 software package for BEAST 2.

research.abstract: The CYP2D6 locus exhibits extensive allelic diversity and structural complexity, complicating the identification of functional variants underlying genetic associations. We previously identified a four-single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) haplotype (AACG) associated with cocaine use disorder and altered CYP2D6 expression in the brain. To characterize the molecular variation of this haplotype, we performed targeted PacBio long-read sequencing on 19 individuals of European ancestry carrying zero, one, or two copies of AACG. Complementary analyses included human pangenome assemblies, protein structural modeling, splice quantitative trait loci, and SNP-array probe sequences. Long-read sequencing resolved distinct CYP2D6 alleles associated with AACG, including CYP2D6 star 2 and star 4. Four of five individuals lacking AACG carried two canonical reference alleles, whereas nearly all AACG homozygotes carried noncanonical alleles. The star 2 allele contained two missense substitutions (R296C and S486T), while star 4 carried four missense substitutions (P34S, L91M, H94R, and S486T) and a loss-of-function splice-site mutation. Structural comparisons suggested potential substrate-dependent effects on ligand binding, while publicly available transcriptomic data associated AACG variants with altered splice-junction usage across multiple tissues, including brain. Although SNP-array intensity differences initially suggested copy-number variation, long-read sequencing did not support consistent gene dosage differences. Instead, polymorphisms within array probe-binding regions provided a plausible explanation for these signals. These findings demonstrate that a disease-associated SNP haplotype tags functionally distinct CYP2D6 alleles and highlight the importance of haplotype-resolved sequencing for interpreting genetic associations at complex pharmacogenomic loci.

research.abstract: Abstract Tarsiers, an elusive family of primates found in Indonesia and the Philippines, sit at an essential point in primate evolution, with their divergence between that of Strepsirrhini (lemurs) and Simiiformes (monkeys and apes). Through homology searches, we have discovered that tarsiers carry the first known case in primates of a gene expansion of protein kinase R (PKR), a kinase involved in the response to viral infection. PKR was quadruplicated in the ancestor of tarsiers and has been maintained since then in all sequenced tarsier species. The extra copies lack the double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) binding domains necessary for detecting viral infection yet largely maintain the residues necessary for the kinase function that carries out PKR’s antiviral function. We show that three of the four PKR copies indeed maintain kinase activity, one of which appears to be resistant to the viral PKR antagonist K3 from vaccinia virus. Our analyses of site and branch-site positive selection reveal that the tarsier PKRs are under positive selection. We propose that these extra copies could serve as a diversification strategy to bypass viral inhibitors that bind PKR’s kinase domain, or they could alternatively serve as decoys that shield the canonical PKR from viral inhibition. This is the first instance of mammal PKR duplicates lacking dsRNA-binding domains and may highlight an innovation in an ancient, long-standing molecular arms race between viruses and a close relative of humans.

research.abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) remains the most economically devastating pathogen of the global swine industry, with frequent genetic recombination and continuous lineage replacement driving its rapid evolution. Hubei Province, a major swine-producing hub in central China, endures substantial PRRSV disease pressure, yet the current epidemiological and evolutionary landscape of circulating strains remains poorly characterized. In this study, 1478 clinical samples were collected from 12 prefecture-level cities between 2024 and 2025 and subjected to RT-PCR detection, ORF5 sequencing, virus isolation, and complete genome analysis. The detection rate among clinical samples was 26.32%, highest in nursery pigs (32.65%). Phylogenetic analysis of 136 ORF5 sequences revealed lineage 1 dominance (66.18%), comprising NADC30-like (38.24%) and NADC34-like (27.94%) strains, followed by lineage 8 (24.26%), lineage 5 (5.15%), and lineage 3 (4.41%). Six isolates were recovered, and whole-genome analysis identified lineage-specific NSP2 deletion patterns and a recombinant strain (LW HP) bearing a JXA1-like backbone with NADC30-like insertions. Selection pressure analysis ranked Nsp2 as the least-constrained gene (dN/dS = 0.3065; purifying selection), with positively selected codons in GP5 and the NSP2 hypervariable region. These findings delineate the current epidemic status and genetic characteristics of PRRSV in central China, providing critical data for regional prevention and vaccine development.

research.abstract: Background Loss to follow-up (LTFU) during tuberculosis treatment is a major programmatic gap, but how much excess mortality it causes has been difficult to estimate, because individuals who disengage differ from those who do not, and they must survive long enough to be recorded as having disengaged. Quantifying this excess and identifying which populations are at greatest risk are critical to informing program design and resource allocation. Methods and findings We followed 171,048 people aged 15 years or older starting a first course of tuberculosis treatment in São Paulo State, Brazil, between 2013 and 2023, linking surveillance and mortality registries; 20,830 (12.2%) were LTFU, defined as interruption of treatment for at least 30 consecutive days. Among those LTFU, 65% had received directly observed therapy (DOT). Using a clone-censor-weight target trial emulation, we contrasted two strategies over 60 months from the first day of treatment: disengagement at any point during the first 6 months and remaining in care throughout. Analyses were adjusted for age, sex, race, education, HIV status, diabetes, alcohol use, drug use, incarceration, homelessness, hospitalization at diagnosis, clinical form of tuberculosis, DOT, and municipality. A rolling landmark analysis addressed the timing of disengagement and cause-specific mortality excess. LTFU increased standardized 5-year mortality by 2.49 percentage points (95% CI [1.94, 3.17]). In a rolling landmark analysis, tuberculosis accounted for 61% of the 5-year excess mortality. Relative effects were largest in younger, stably housed individuals, whose baseline mortality was low; the largest absolute excess fell on people living with HIV (5.16 percentage points, 95% CI [3.76, 6.60]). The excess was similar for disengagement at any point in the first 4 months of treatment and attenuated thereafter. Limitations include the absence from the registry of severity markers such as radiographic extent and bacillary load, so residual confounding cannot be excluded. Conclusions Despite high DOT coverage, disengagement during the first 6 months of tuberculosis treatment was common and increased 5-year mortality under the stated identification assumptions, with the excess concentrated in deaths attributed to tuberculosis. Interventions that provide support throughout treatment should be tested for their effectiveness in sustaining engagement and reducing mortality.

research.abstract: Background: Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) remains the most lethal central nervous system (CNS) infection in neurosurgical practice, with case fatality rates of 25–50% despite appropriate therapy. Up to 80% of TBM patients develop hydrocephalus, and outcomes in advanced disease are determined primarily by the timing of anti-tuberculous therapy (ATT) rather than the method of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) diversion. We report a fatal case of isolated CNS tuberculosis (TB) complicated by aqueductal stenosis-induced obstructive hydrocephalus, in which a systemic diagnostic delay, driven by the requirement for microbiological confirmation before ATT could be dispensed, cascaded into delayed medical and surgical management and was the principal determinant of outcome rather than surgical technique. Case Description: A 26-year-old human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-negative Egyptian male presented with recurrent high-grade fever, neck stiffness, diplopia, and urinary retention. CSF showed high protein (306.7 mg/ dL), low glucose (42.1 mg/dL), and lymphocytic pleocytosis (400 cells/mm 3 ), with negative Ziehl–Neelsen stain and BioFire ME panel, which does not include Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB). Despite a CSF profile suggestive of TBM, GeneXpert MTB/rifampicin Ultra was not performed and ATT was deferred pending polymerase chain reaction confirmation. Dexamethasone was started appropriately on day 1. Computed tomography (CT) brain showed ventricular dilatation, but neurosurgical consultation was not obtained. CT chest later showed no pulmonary involvement, supporting isolated CNS TB. On Day 5, the patient deteriorated to Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) 6–7 with seizures; emergency external ventricular drain (EVD) was inserted and ATT initiated on day 6, approximately 36 days after symptom onset. He subsequently developed steroid-induced diabetic ketoacidosis and severe hypernatremia consistent with central diabetes insipidus. Despite EVD and ATT, neurological status progressed to GCS 2T with absent brainstem reflexes, and he died approximately 10 days after EVD insertion. Conclusion: This case illustrates three critical failures: (1) neurosurgical consultation was reactive rather than proactive – initiated upon seizures and coma rather than upon CT evidence of hydrocephalus; (2) CSF diversion without concurrent ATT is temporizing, not curative – ongoing meningeal inflammation will progress regardless of EVD adequacy; and (3) a negative syndromic molecular panel that lacks MTB coverage must not delay empirical ATT when the CSF profile is unambiguous. The EVD was technically appropriate and correctly positioned; the therapeutic window had already closed before surgery was performed. In Medical Research Council Grade III TBM, outcome is determined by ATT timing and disease severity at presentation, not by the specific method of CSF diversion.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Positive selection shapes protein function by favoring amino acid substitutions that increase fitness. Although numerous studies have identified positively selected genes (PSGs), the structural principles underlying residue-level positive selection remain incompletely understood and previous studies have produced conflicting conclusions, particularly regarding the preferential location of positively selected residues (PSRs) within intrinsically disordered regions. In order to resolve these issues and to better understand the driving forces underlying positive selection in human proteins, we performed a comprehensive analysis on a manually curated, high quality collection of PSGs and PSRs as well as on a large-scale PSR dataset restricted to proteins with experimental structures. Results Human PSRs were significantly enriched in secreted and cell membrane proteins and preferentially localized to extracellular regions, solvent-exposed protein surfaces, coil structures, and protein-protein interaction interfaces, whereas neither domains nor intrinsically disordered regions showed an enrichment. Spatial clustering analysis reinforced that PSRs accumulate within localized surface patches. Integration of host-pathogen interaction data highlighted that adaptive changes preferentially affect extracellular molecular recognition surfaces, recurrently appearing in certain pathogen-interacting membrane protein families and particular domain types. Additionally, PSRs showed an enrichment in the residues of human-pathogen interaction interfaces that are in direct contact with pathogenic proteins, implying that neutralizing pathogen attacks is one of the driving forces behind the adaptive evolution of human proteins. By analysing human variation data we found that PSRs are enriched in benign but depleted in pathogenic substitutions, extending previous observations that positively selected genes contain elevated levels of missense variation. Notably, PSGs of the large-scale dataset were also enriched among clinical-stage drug targets, suggesting a potential link between positive selection and pharmacological relevance. Conclusion Together, our results provide a refined structural model of adaptive evolution in human proteins and identify extracellular exposed molecular recognition surfaces and human-pathogen interaction interfaces as recurrent hotspots of positive selection. Our results point to the direction that precise identification of human PSRs could delineate important host-pathogen interfaces that exert evolutionary selection pressure on humans and appoint novel targets with therapeutic potential.

research.abstract: Introduction A substantial proportion of people with tuberculosis (TB) do not experience or report typical symptoms. We aimed to describe the characteristics of people with asymptomatic TB disease (aTB) and compare its proportion among people diagnosed with TB during community-wide active case finding (ACF) and passive case finding (PCF) in Vietnam. Methods We undertook a cohort study in Ca Mau Province, Vietnam, comparing people with pulmonary TB detected through community-wide ACF using rapid molecular testing irrespective of symptoms, and those diagnosed through routine care at district health facilities (PCF) over the same period. We defined aTB as TB disease without symptoms, based on a post-diagnosis questionnaire. Secondary analyses applied alternative aTB definitions: absence of WHO 4-symptoms and cough for ≥2 weeks. We used modified Poisson regression with robust sandwich variance to quantify the prevalence ratio for aTB in ACF versus PCF. Results Asymptomatic disease was present in 0.9% (PCF) and 12.9% (ACF) of people diagnosed with TB. People with aTB showed lower culture positivity and Xpert Mycobacterium tuberculosis/rifampicin semi-quantitative levels. However, >70% had chest X-ray findings consistent with TB. Compared to PCF, ACF-detected cases were more likely to lack symptoms under each definition: adjusted prevalence ratios for aTB were 13.7 [95%CI 3.2-58.7] for asymptomatic, 2.6 [95%CI 1.6-4.5] for WHO 4-symptoms, and 1.9 [95%CI 1.3-2.8] for cough ≥2 weeks. Conclusion Community-wide ACF detected a significantly higher proportion of aTB than PCF. Screening strategies that require symptoms as a prerequisite are likely to miss a substantial proportion of people with TB.

research.abstract: PREPRINT-32 (v1.0.0 Empirical Preprint) • 100% Native Rust Partitioned ModelTest Across 433 Verified Records Understanding how the eukaryotic nucleus emerged from archaeal ancestors requires resolving deep archaeal-eukaryotic relationships alongside the evolutionary conservation of nuclear transport, chromatin, and membrane-remodeling machinery. Here, we analyzed 433 verified NCBI sequence records across 64 species using a partitioned 18-locus supermatrix (26,387 aligned base pairs) with third-codon RY recoding and multispecies coalescent reconciliation across 5,880,795 gene-tree quartets. Per-locus model selection and RY recoding reduced compositional bias by 83.6% (to RCFV 0.0236) and improved log-likelihood by +8013.3 units over an unpartitioned model, raising mean bootstrap support across the 52 species meeting the 65% completeness threshold (at least 8 loci) from 84.0% for a single locus to 95.1%, with strong gene-tree coalescent concordance (normalized quartet score Q = 0.73, mean posterior probability 0.81). Relaxed-clock dating places the Archaeal Root at 3.24 billion years ago, the Asgard-FECA Nuclear Stem at 2.99 billion years ago, the LECA Crown Radiation at 1.98 billion years ago, and the SAR Supergroup Crown Radiation at 1.45 billion years ago. Across 4 conserved protein families (47 orthologs), codon models reveal pervasive purifying selection (dN/dS = 0.031-0.101), while 3D structural alignment against PDB 1BYU confirms high fold conservation (TM-score 0.978) alongside 12 single-species Bayesian demographic reconstructions (322 isolates). An 18-locus phylogenomic study of 64 species traces the origin of the eukaryotic nucleus from Asgardarchaeota to crown eukaryotes (stem 2.99 Ga, crown 1.98 Ga; 95.1% mean bootstrap, Q = 0.73) and conserved protein structure. research.abstract: Direct genome sequencing of Mycoplasma genitalium from clinical specimens is challenging due to the organism′s low bacterial load. We developed and compared two DNA enrichment strategies – amplicon-based and hybridisation capture-based – coupled with next-generation sequencing, and assessed the suitability of DNA capture for whole-genome sequencing and high-resolution molecular typing. The enrichment approaches, RNA bait hybridisation and targeted sequence amplification, were combined with paired-end sequencing on the Illumina iSeq 100. Method performance was evaluated in 89 M. genitalium -positive specimens across five genomic loci: 23S and 16S rRNA, and parC and gyrA for macrolide, tetracycline, and fluoroquinolone resistance, respectively, and mgpB for phylogenetic analysis. Regarding antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants, the multiplex amplicon sequencing method demonstrated the highest sensitivity, at 93.3-98.9%. Although < 50% of samples were characterised using DNA capture, concordance between the two methods was excellent. Using DNA capture, 24.7% of specimens achieved a minimum coverage of 95% at 1× depth. Sequencing success was inversely correlated with human DNA contamination and the presence of low-quality reads. Whole-genome single-nucleotide polymorphism analysis provided higher discriminatory power than multi-locus sequence typing schemes and confirmed the clonality of multidrug-resistant M. genitalium strains belonging to the mgpB genotype 159. In conclusion, targeted amplicon-based enrichment is the most accurate and reliable approach for epidemiological studies focused on AMR and mgpB typing, whereas DNA capture is valuable for generating comprehensive genomic data from selected M. genitalium -positive specimens.

research.abstract: DEG (Degradation of periplasmic proteins) proteases are ATP-independent serine endopeptidases found in bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes including plants. They are considered to be key regulators of development and stress tolerance in plants. In this study, a comprehensive genome-wide analysis identified 19 serine protease-like DEG family proteins in potato (Solanum tuberosum L.), revealing their structural diversity, domain architecture, and regulatory potential. Physiochemical profiling showed a predominance of acidic isoelectric points (pI), variable protein lengths (169–1083 amino acids), and differential stability indices. Subcellular localization predicted most DEG proteases to reside in the chloroplast, with others distributed across cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, and peroxisome. Domain analysis confirmed the universal presence of the trypsin domain, with varying numbers of PDZ domains and additional conserved motifs among paralogs. Evolutionary divergence analysis of StDEG genes and their orthologs from six Solanaceae species as well as Arabidopsis thaliana, Oryza sativa, and Zea mays revealed dN/dS ratios below one for all orthologous pairs, suggesting that StDEG genes have evolved under strong purifying selection and remained highly conserved throughout plant evolution. Gene ontology annotations linked DEG proteases to key biological functions including PSII repair, photoinhibition, and chloroplast organization, alongside protein catabolism and light stimulus response. Promoter analysis revealed an abundance of cis-regulatory elements (CREs), particularly light-responsive motifs, along with hormone and stress-related elements such as ABRE, ARE, and MBS. Expression profiling across eight developmental tissues demonstrated tissue-specific expression patterns, with strong transcript accumulation of selected DEG members in senescent leaf, stolon, shoot apex, and tuber. Interestingly, several splice variants showed unique expression dynamics, including stage-specific and stress-induced activation. Upon exposure to abiotic and hormonal cues, 16 DEG proteases displayed significant transcriptional modulation, particularly under light, ABA, and Zeatin treatments, with notable fold changes reaching up to 26-fold in certain variants. These findings highlight the functional versatility of DEG proteases in potato development and stress adaptation, especially their responsiveness to light and hormonal stimuli. The characterization of these proteases paves the way for future studies on their roles in crop resilience and genome editing applications.

research.abstract: Abstract Enteropathogenic and enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EPEC/EHEC) cause severe global diarrhoeal disease, exacerbated by rising antimicrobial resistance. Pathogenesis relies on ‘attaching and effacing’ lesions, where bacteria generate actin pedestals to adhere, replicate, and destroy intestinal microvilli. To identify novel anti-virulence candidates targeting this process, we conducted a high-throughput phenotypic screen quantifying pedestal formation via high-content fluorescence microscopy. We identified the anticancer nucleotide analogue clofarabine as a potent inhibitor of EPEC growth and pathogenesis. Distinct from its oncology mechanism - inducing DNA chain termination and apoptosis - clofarabine competes with bacterial ATP-dependent processes to impede gene transcription, protein synthesis, and Type III Secretion System (T3SS) function. Remarkably, EPEC counteracts this inhibition by cleaving clofarabine, enabling restored protein synthesis and resumed growth. Furthermore, we report for the first time that clofarabine suppresses protein translation in human monocytes, suggesting an uncharacterised translational impact on mammalian cells. These findings reveal host and bacterial translation as interconnected vulnerabilities to purine antimetabolites, offering a novel strategy to disarm enteric pathogens while uncovering a bacterial enzymatic mechanism for neutralizing host-targeted therapeutics.

research.abstract: Undernutrition is the leading risk factor for tuberculosis susceptibility, severity, and poor treatment outcome. Nutritional immunology and immunometabolism frame how nutrient availability and metabolism shape host defense against Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( Mtb ) infection. By integrating targeted metabolomics and transcriptional profiling in a murine tuberculosis model, we defined immunometabolic programs underlying the transition from acute to chronic infection. Immune control of Mtb during acute infection was accompanied by robust activation of immune and metabolic programs, including mTORC1-associated signaling, glutaminolysis, glycolysis, arginine metabolism, and serine one-carbon metabolism, thereby highlighting the importance of amino acid metabolism and mitochondrial function in antimicrobial immunity. In contrast, chronic infection was characterized by reduced immune activation and mTORC1-associated signaling, increased branched-chain amino acid catabolism, and altered amino acid profiles, with leucine and glutamine among the discriminating metabolites. These findings suggest that reduced glutamine availability during chronic infection may increase reliance on leucine oxidative catabolism to sustain mitochondrial metabolism during nutrient stress, potentially limiting leucine availability for mTORC1-associated anabolic metabolism and immune activation. Oral glutamine supplementation restored amino acid homeostasis, including lung leucine abundance, enhanced mTORC1-associated signaling and central metabolic programs, moderately reduced bacterial burden and lung pathology, and mitigated infection-associated wasting. Reanalysis of published human metabolomics datasets further demonstrated reduced circulating glutamine levels during progression to active tuberculosis, supporting conservation of glutamine metabolic dysregulation across host species. Collectively, our findings identify a potential glutamine–leucine metabolic axis linking nutrient availability with immunometabolic competence and provide a mechanistic rationale for evaluating glutamine supplementation as a host-directed strategy for tuberculosis.

research.abstract: The GRAS gene family, a plant-specific family of transcription factors, plays critical roles in diverse developmental processes and abiotic stress responses. Although extensive studies on the identification and functional characterization of GRAS genes have been conducted in numerous plant species, systematic analyses of this family in Salvia miltiorrhiza, a valuable traditional Chinese medicinal herb, remain limited. The present study aims to identify and characterize GRAS genes in S. miltiorrhiza, thereby providing a comprehensive understanding of their phylogenetic evolution, functional divergence, and tissue-specific expression profiles​. In this study, a total of 33 GRAS genes were identified in S. miltiorrhiza and subjected to comprehensive analysis. Phylogenetic analysis classified these genes into eight distinct subgroups and identified eight pairs of paralogs. Genetic divergence analysis revealed that the GRAS gene family has predominantly undergone purifying selection, as evidenced by Ka/Ks ratios below 1 for all eight paralogous pairs. Positive selection analysis using the site and branch-site models further suggested that SmGRAS genes had gone through purifying selective pressure for adaptive evolution. Motif analysis showed that group-specific motifs likely contribute to functional divergence among subgroups. Functional divergence analysis suggested that subgroup-specific genes may have experienced functional divergence during evolution, and provided preliminary insights into the molecular mechanisms potentially underlying their divergent functions. Tissue-specific expression analysis revealed that SmGRAS genes might perform distinct functions in different tissues. This study presents a comprehensive characterization of the GRAS gene family in S. miltiorrhiza. Taken together, these results elucidate a comprehensive understanding of the GRAS gene family and furnish robust references for subsequent functional investigations of GRAS genes in S. miltiorrhiza.

research.abstract: Background Members of the Triatoma brasiliensis species complex are among the primary vectors of Chagas disease in northeastern Brazil. Despite their epidemiological importance, mitogenomic resources for this group remain limited, constraining comparative and evolutionary analyses at the genomic scale. Methods We assembled and annotated twelve near-complete mitochondrial genomes representing four taxa of the T. brasiliensis complex ( T. b. brasiliensis , T. melanica , T. sherlocki , and T. petrocchiae ), with three specimens per taxon. Genome annotation and gene-specific analyses were conducted to assess patterns of sequence and structural variation across taxa. A concatenated dataset including protein-coding genes, rRNAs, and tRNAs was analyzed under a partitioned maximum likelihood framework, with partitions defined by gene and codon position. Results All mitogenomes exhibited the canonical insect gene complement and gene order. Genome length variation (16,277–17,238 bp) involved variation in non-coding regions, including the A + T-rich control region and an expanded intergenic spacer between tRNA-Ser(UCN) and ND1 in T. petrocchiae, driven by tandem repeats. Among protein-coding genes, ND6 showed the highest nucleotide variability and elevated amino-acid variability relative to most other mitochondrial genes, with structural differences among the examined taxa. Phylogenetic analyses recovered the sampled members of the T. brasiliensis species complex as a fully supported monophyletic clade. Conclusion The marked variation observed in ND6, including distinct amino-acid motifs among the examined specimens, suggests that this gene may contain potentially informative variation for lineage-level evolutionary studies. However, the restricted geographic sampling, the limited number of specimens per taxon, and the incomplete representation of the T. brasiliensis complex constrain the generalizability of these findings. Broader geographic and taxonomic sampling will be required to determine the consistency and taxonomic significance of these patterns, while the mitogenomic dataset as a whole expands the resources available for investigating mitochondrial diversity and evolutionary relationships in Triatominae.

research.abstract: The convention that mutation is a random process has been challenged by suggestions that selection has acted on between-gene variation in the mutation rate, with claims that more important genes are protected from mutation in part, in prokaryotes, by being on the leading strand, while those required for rapid adaptive evolution have higher mutation rates, in part by being on the lagging strand. The original selectionist claims have proven contentious with several replication failures. However, none of the replication attempts fully allow for covariates and many employ data from mismatch repair (MMR) knockout strains. To address these limitations, we consider amassed mutation accumulation data for wild-type Escherichia coli , the focal species for adaptive claims, and Saccharomyces cerevisiae , in a multiple parameter-controlled analysis to predict between-gene variation in mutational density (mutations per base pair). Along with covariates, we consider putative selectively relevant parameters: protein level and essentiality to capture genic “importance”, and, in E. coli , strand with respect to DNA replication. We consider deviation of correlation and partial correlation values from those expected under trinucleotide-controlled simulations. While in E. coli more highly transcribed genes may have slightly lower mutation rates, potentially consistent with a selectionist model, the same is not seen in yeast, and in neither species do genes for more abundant or essential proteins have lower mutation rates. In E. coli there is no difference in mutation rate between genes on different strands, a lack of difference replicated in other prokaryotes. The degree of purifying selection is also not predictive of mutation density. We additionally highlight a strong artefact seen using the standard off-the-shelf statistical approach and note that results from MMR-deficient strains are discordant. We conclude that as trends are nearly uniformly unsupportive, not consistent between species and of miniscule effect size, they present no challenge to convention.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: India, the capital of tuberculosis (TB) worldwide, accounts for 27% of the global burden of drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). Managing DR-TB in itself is challenging, and preexisting multiorgan dysfunction makes it even more lengthy and complex. Here, we share our real-world experience in successfully managing a difficult-to-treat case of rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB), a type of DR-TB, in a high-risk patient with multiple comorbidities. CASE PRESENTATION: A 60-year-old 70 kg male diagnosed with RR-TB was referred from a District DR-TB Centre to our Nodal DR-TB Centre for pretreatment evaluation and treatment initiation in December 2022. Baseline evaluation revealed severe renal dysfunction, hepatic dysfunction, a prolonged QT interval, and poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, necessitating an individualized all-oral longer regimen with appropriate dose adjustments guided by the National Programmatic Management of Drug-resistant Tuberculosis Guidelines. During treatment, the regimen was sequentially individualized in response to evolving suspected adverse drug reactions, with each modification aimed at optimizing patient safety while maintaining an effective treatment regimen. The patient showed radiological improvement, achieved sputum culture conversion, and successfully completed the 18-month treatment by June 2024. The patient did not relapse during the 18-month follow-up period (December 2025). CONCLUSION: This case report exemplifies the success of personalized pharmacotherapeutic decision-making in challenging cases. Structured toxicity assessment and intensive clinical, laboratory, and electrocardiography monitoring in addition to timely treatment modification may facilitate successful treatment in carefully selected high-risk RR-TB patients when standard regimens are not feasible, even in resource-limited settings. research.abstract: Abstract Bacterial genomic analysis is a cornerstone of modern epidemiology. Many genomic typing methods exist, and most are designed to work within a given species in a hierarchical fashion. However, designation of bacterial species can be problematic, making the higher resolution level of hierarchical typing difficult. Using the universally present ribosomal proteins, we have developed a pipeline for a robust typing system which can be used to assign an unknown organism to a species-level cluster or, sometimes, a sub-species cluster. As proof of principle, we have used bacterial genomes from the genus Campylobacter , the most common cause of human bacterial gastroenteritis within which new strains, and new species ( C. infantis ), are reported. Species assignment, of all but the two most common species C. jejuni and C. coli , is beyond the ability of most microbiology laboratories. Outbreak investigation, even with genomic data, is difficult and so a robust typing scheme would be useful. Using available sequence-based typing schemes, we attempted to differentiate between 39 published Campylobacter species; we determined that the ribosomal 16S sequence typing and SNP typing did not discriminate all 39 but a single gene phylogeny method ( gyrB ), BUSCO, Mash, Panaroo and use of the Hug proteins differentiated all 39. We assessed computational accessibility (important for implementation) and biological applicability (one universal typing scheme is easier to validate). The application of Hug proteins proved computationally efficient and should be widely applicable. We developed a workflow in snakemake and Python, capable of clustering thousands of bacterial genomes. This Robust Cluster (RC) typing workflow was made accessible via the Terra platform, with usage instructions provided through an online training course on YouTube. Ninety-eight Campylobacter isolates from Bangladesh were sequenced and analysed using the Terra workflow, resulting in the identification of several novel clusters not previously found among publicly available genomes. Our work establishes the availability of RC typing and demonstrates its capacity to identify new Campylobacter lineages, thereby facilitating reporting and supporting future research initiatives.

research.abstract: Abstract Darwinian evolution has produced two types of functional polymers with different chemical alphabets, RNA and proteins. Dominance of proteins across many cellular functions in extant organisms has been classically attributed to catalytic superiority over RNA. From this perspective, functional RNAs are fossils from the origin of life, where they possibly kick-started molecular evolution. Yet, in addition to direct catalytic capability, the chemical alphabets of RNA and proteins give rise to distinct evolving codes. A crucial question is therefore how the evolution of functional structures is shaped by mutational variation for each of these codes. Here, we employ RNAfold and ESMFold structure predictions to directly compare mutational profiles— i.e . the distribution of secondary structures upon point mutations—of functional RNA and proteins. Unlike RNA, natural protein structures feature a narrow mutational profile with high mutational robustness but limited structural variation. Moreover, while functional and random RNA sequences share similar mutational profiles, secondary structures of natural proteins are substantially more robust than those of random sequences and de novo proteins, revealing an evolutionary drive toward robustness. Integrating structure prediction with phylogenetic data and simulations, we find evidence for the hypothesis that robust protein structures are favored by selection to buffer errors in translation. As a side-effect, the propensity for structural innovation is reduced in proteins. Our results show that protein folds have evolutionary properties distinct from RNA structures, with implications for the origin of function in both types of molecules—in present-day organisms, as well as during the origin of life. Significance statement How changes in RNA and protein sequences propagate to their structure through the folding process is fundamental to understanding the evolutionary behavior and functional potential of these polymers. Using computational structure predictions, we argue that protein structures have been selected to exhibit high robustness to translation errors, which, as a side-effect, limits access to structural variants for evolutionary innovation. In stark contrast, RNA structures are innately robust and evolvable, and show no signature of selection. Our work thus shows how mutational effects can be molded by evolution for fixed genotype-phenotype maps. In maps that themselves evolve, such as gene regulatory networks, the imprint of past selection is likely even stronger.

research.abstract: Abstract The Wnt gene family plays a central role in vertebrate development, yet its evolutionary dynamics across lineages remain largely unexplored. Here, we present the most comprehensive analysis of Wnt gene evolution in vertebrates to date, leveraging a large-scale comparative genomics approach of 38,886 Wnt gene sequences mined from 1,961 species. We first investigate overall patterns of gene retention, duplication, and loss, and then focus specifically on the impact of whole-genome duplications (WGDs). We uncover striking variation in Wnt gene repertoire sizes, with ray-finned fishes (Actinopterygii) exhibiting the largest repertoires – even after excluding taxa with recent WGDs. Notably, we identify extreme expansions in polyploid cyprinids, including an octoploid hybrid harbouring 99 Wnt genes, the highest number observed. Unexpectedly elevated Wnt copy numbers in diploid species, such as in the Antarctic lanternfish (Electrona antarctica) and the brook lamprey (Lethenteron reissneri), point to lineage-specific expansions, although the potential adaptive significance of these expansions remains to be tested. Evolutionary rate analyses reveal that certain Wnt clades – especially Wnt8 and Wnt16 – exhibit elevated dN/dS ratios and high birth–death rates, consistent with repeated episodes of relaxed constraint and/or adaptive diversification. Contrary to our expectations, there was no relationship between developmental expression timing and evolutionary rates, suggesting pleiotropic regulation and functional redundancy of Wnt genes. Altogether, our findings reveal widespread variation in Wnt copy number and turnover among lineages, shaped by both genome duplication history and divergent evolutionary trajectories. This work provides a high-resolution framework for understanding the molecular evolution of a key developmental toolkit and highlights candidate genes for future studies of vertebrate eco-morphological diversity.

research.abstract: Transformer-based foundation models have shown strong potential for modeling longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), yet existing models focus primarily on risk prediction rather than treatment effect estimation, which limits evidence generation. Here, we introduce the ITE-Transformer, a transformer-based framework that combines self-supervised representation learning from longitudinal patient trajectories with doubly robust causal machine learning for predicting individualized treatment effects (ITEs). As a result, our ITE-Transformer allows to study counterfactual questions of how an individual patient's outcome may differ under alternative treatment strategies. The ITE-Transformer learns temporally contextualized representations of patients' diagnosis and medication histories and subsequently uses these representations to predict treatment assignment, treatment-specific outcome risks, and patient-specific ITEs. The ITE-Transformer is trained using structured EHR data from ~350,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program and evaluated in two clinically different comparative-effectiveness tasks: (i) GLP-1 receptor agonists versus DPP-4 inhibitors among patients with type 2 diabetes, with major adverse cardiovascular events as the outcome, and (ii) immunotherapy versus chemotherapy in a pan-cancer cohort, with all-cause mortality as the outcome. Across both applications, the ITE-Transformer improves the discrimination and calibration of treatment assignment and outcome models compared with existing tabular machine learning approaches and an otherwise identical transformer trained without self-supervised pre-training. The ITE-Transformer further identifies substantial heterogeneity in predicted ITEs and yields interpretable patterns of treatment response associated with patients' diagnoses, medication histories, and comorbidities. Together, our work demonstrates how clinical foundation models can be developed for analyzing heterogeneity in treatment effects and thus support real-world evidence generation.

We analyzed severity metrics, demographics, clinical, microbiological, radiological, household and behavioral data for their association with and their ability to predict culture conversion. The highest CXR Score category (odds ratio (OR) 0.51, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) 0.31, 0.84), smear grade at diagnosis (OR 0.42, 95% CI; 0.26, 0.62), pleural thickening (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.17, 0.95) and current smoking (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.09, 0.99) inversely associated with conversion. Conclusion CXR Score, higher smear grade at diagnosis, pleural thickening, and current smoking inversely associated with culture conversion but provided limited utility for prediction.

research.abstract: Computing phylogenetic likelihoods becomes challenging when the continuous-time Markov chain has a large state space. At each branch, pruning algorithms require terms of the form $e^{Q t}\cdot B$, where $Q$ is an $S \times S$ rate matrix (e.g., for $S$ states), $t$ is a branch length, and the columns of matrix $B$ (e.g., $B \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{S \times L}$) are partial-likelihood vectors for $L$ site patterns. Many implementations calculate the dense transition matrix $P(t)=e^{Q t}$ via eigendecomposition and multiply it by $B$. This strategy is efficient for small state spaces, but it can be inefficient for large sparse rate matrices because forming $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices destroys sparsity and its cost may not be well amortized when $L$ is small. We implement an alternative likelihood kernel based on the Al-Mohy and Higham (2011) algorithm for computing the action of the matrix exponential directly, avoiding explicit construction of $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices. The resulting method takes full advantage of the sparsity of $Q$. We implement this method as a CPU-based extension to the BEAGLE library and evaluate it on two large-state molecular models: a Markov-modulated codon model of heterotachy with $M$ selective regimes and $61\cdot M$ possible states, and a codon-pair model of interlocus gene conversion between two paralogs with $61^2=3\,721$ possible states. Our results characterize when action-based likelihood computation improves performance over calculating $e^{Q t}$ directly. We show that this method enables fast, scalable inference for complex models, removing a key computational barrier to the study of evolution with large state space models.

research.abstract: Oropouche virus caused an unprecedented epidemic across the Americas during 2023-2025, associated with the expansion of the reassortant M1L2S2 lineage. To investigate its dissemination, we develop the Birth-Death Exposed-Infectious Vector-Human (BDEIVH) model within a deep-learning framework that explicitly represents alternating human-vector transmission and incubation periods. The model defines two directional reproduction numbers, RVH and RHV, whose product, RHH, quantifies the expected number of secondary human infections generated by a single infectious human through one complete transmission cycle. In simulations, BDEIVH provides more accurate RHH estimates than conventional birth-death models, with predictive accuracy improving with phylogeny size and remaining robust under reduced phylogenetic resolution. Across three major Brazilian OROV genomic clusters, estimated durations of infection range from 15.4 to 18.5 days in vectors and from 9.42 to 12.3 days in humans, whereas whole-cluster RHH estimates range from 1.15 to 1.81. RHH estimates reached a peak of 4.4 in the endemic Amazon region and 3.0 in the non-endemic Atlantic Forest region. These findings show that explicitly modelling vector-mediated transmission improves phylodynamic inference and reveals substantial OROV transmission in both endemic and non-endemic regions.

research.abstract: Population heterogeneity challenges the transportability of prediction models. Transfer learning may improve prediction through information borrowing, but its utility across population settings remains unclear. We evaluated a regression-based transfer learning framework across international aging cohorts (Gateway) and race/ethnicity groups within the RAND Health and Retirement Study (RAND HRS). Gateway included 19,879 adults with diabetes from eight cohorts, while RAND HRS included 3,926 participants across four race/ethnicity groups. Prediction models for patient-reported health outcomes were developed using demographic and clinical risk factors. Transfer learning was compared with target-only and pooled models using AUC and Brier score, with bootstrap resampling to assess uncertainty. Transfer learning improved prediction in 75% (6/8) of Gateway cohorts, with AUC gains of 0.1%-0.6%, and in all four RAND HRS race/ethnicity groups, with gains of 0.8%-3.1%. Improvements were greater and more consistent across within-cohort groups. These findings demonstrate the potential of regression-based transfer learning to improve prediction across heterogeneous populations. Information borrowing from sufficiently transferable external data may enhance prediction performance and provide meaningful public health benefits, even when improvements are modest, particularly in large population-based cohorts.

research.abstract: H14 avian influenza viruses (AIVs) are rare, with limited data on their circulation in mainland China. This study investigated the ecological origins and zoonotic potential of H14 viruses in southern China. The isolates were characterised by full-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analysis, together with assessment of avian- and human-type receptor binding, in vitro replication in avian, mammalian, and human cell lines, and in vivo pathogenicity in mice. Four H14 AIVs (one H14N6, two H14N7, and one H14N8) were isolated. We identified a novel H14 transmission network involving Mareca penelope and various shorebird species, indicating a multihost dispersal mechanism. Guangdong isolates formed a distinct subclade within the Eurasian lineage, closely related to Russian and Cambodian strains. The isolates (SZ3742/H14N6, ZJ3523/H14N7, SZ3536/H14N8) exhibited dual receptor-binding specificity for avian (α-2,3) and human (α-2,6) sialic acids. Strain-dependent replication in human A549 cells showed SZ3742/H14N6 peaked comparably to DF-1 cells but lower than MDCK cells, while the others had lower peak titres. All isolates replicated transiently at low titres in mouse lungs with limited pathogenicity. Molecular characterisation revealed mammalian adaptation markers and a typical HA cleavage site motif (PDKQTR↓GLF). This study presents the first evidence of H14 AIV circulation in Guangdong, emphasising the need for enhanced surveillance in the East Asian -Australasian Flyway.

research.abstract: Phylogenetic trees are hybrid objects: branch lengths vary continuously, while topologies change discretely through edge contractions and expansions. Billera-Holmes-Vogtmann (BHV) tree space provides a canonical geometry for this structure, representing each resolved topology as a Euclidean orthant and topological changes as motion across shared lower-dimensional boundaries. We introduce PhylaFlow, a hybrid flow-matching model that learns posterior-basin transport in BHV tree space. PhylaFlow is trained on BHV geodesic paths from random starting trees to short-run posterior samples, coupling continuous branch-length motion within orthants with learned boundary events and discrete topology transitions. We evaluate the learned geometry operationally: if the flow reaches posterior-relevant regions, finite-budget Bayesian refinement initialized from, or guided by, its terminal trees should recover posterior-supported topologies more efficiently. Across DS1-DS8 phylogenetic posterior benchmarks, PhylaFlow substantially reduces initial Tree-KL relative to classical initializers. After finite-budget MrBayes refinement, direct PhylaFlow improves early and intermediate topology-recovery trajectories on most datasets, while split-guided PhylaFlow-MCMC obtains the strongest hard-case results. The best PhylaFlow variant outperforms short-warmup on seven of eight datasets and PhyloGFN on five of eight under the same refinement budget. In a joint sequence-conditioned experiment, sequence embeddings steer posterior split recovery, although exact posterior topology recovery remains preliminary. These results show that hybrid flow matching can learn actionable transport in BHV tree space and provide a geometry-aware proposal mechanism for Bayesian phylogenetic inference.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT The leech gut is known to be a viral reservoir, where viruses can persist long-term and are protected from external influences. Therefore, leeches can serve as vectors for transmission of viral disease to susceptible hosts on which they prey. Nonetheless, viral diversity and virus-leech-host interactions remain largely unknown, with hitherto no research directed at identifying viruses that use leeches as their hosts. In the present study, we report the discovery of a novel large DNA virus (phylum Nucleocytoviricota ) recovered from genomic sequencing data of the common fish leech Piscicola geometra (Linnaeus, 1761). Through genomic and phylogenetic analyses, we identify this lineage as highly divergent from currently known viruses, with ~95% of its predicted protein-coding genes showing no identifiable homology with current databases. Whether the leech is a host of this virus or a vector that transmits it to fish species remains to be investigated. This work highlights the value of off-target sequence retrieval for discovering novel viral lineages and sets the stage for future studies directed towards the prevalence and biology of leech-associated large DNA viruses.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Glucocorticoid-induced diabetes mellitus (GIDM) is a frequent but under-documented complication of systemic corticosteroid therapy. We aimed to estimate its incidence and identify patient- and treatment-related risk factors. Methods We conducted a retrospective, single-centre cohort study in the Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine A, Charles Nicolle Hospital, Tunis, between January 2000 and December 2020. Ninety-five adults without known diabetes (baseline HbA1c < 6.5%) starting corticosteroid therapy were followed for GIDM. Univariate predictors (p < 0.05) were entered into a multivariable model. Results Mean age was 42.6 years (M/F ratio 0.79). GIDM developed in 57 of 95 patients (60%), after a median of 20 days (range 7–120); 40% of cases occurred within the first month. The median initial dose was 60 mg/day prednisone-equivalent, and 84% received high-dose therapy. On univariate analysis, older age, family history of type 2 diabetes, higher baseline fasting glucose, higher body weight, and methylprednisolone boluses were associated with GIDM; sex, body mass index and hypertension were not. After adjustment, only family history of type 2 diabetes (RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.18–2.61) and higher baseline fasting glucose (RR 1.37 per 1 mmol/L, 95% CI 1.07–1.75) remained independent predictors. Conclusion GIDM occurred in three-fifths of patients, usually within the first month of therapy. Family history of type 2 diabetes and baseline fasting glucose independently identify patients warranting glycaemic surveillance from treatment initiation.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains the leading infectious killer worldwide. Brazil is among the 30 high-burden TB countries, however, genomic surveillance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains remains limited. We analyzed a convenience sample of 350 clinical isolates collected between 2016 and 2021 in metropolitan Rio de Janeiro to investigate genomic diversity, drug resistance and transmission dynamics. Among the isolates, 302 were phenotypically susceptible, while 48 showed resistance to at least one drug, including 35 multidrug-resistant (MDR) cases. Whole-genome sequencing predictions showed high concordance with phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (rifampicin 99%, isoniazid 99%, ethambutol 98%, streptomycin 97%). The most common resistance mutations were katG Ser315Thr and rpoB Ser450Leu. All isolates belonged to Lineage 4, predominantly sub-lineages 4.1 (Haarlem) and 4.3 (Latin American-Mediterranean). Despite incomplete sampling, genomic analysis identified 28 transmission clusters involving 23.2% of isolates, including a large MDR-TB cluster in the Tijuca neighborhood. Multi-year clusters indicated continued detection of closely related isolates over time, suggesting the persistence of related genomic lineages. No association was observed between resistance-associated mutations and treatment outcomes, although these analyses were likely underpowered to detect such associations. These findings highlight the need to strengthen genomic surveillance, molecular diagnostics, contact tracing, and treatment follow-up to control TB in the region.

research.abstract: Introduction Abutilon fruticosum Guill. & Perr. is a drought-tolerant Malvaceae subshrub native to Saudi Arabia. However, no mitochondrial genome has previously been reported for the genus Abutilon . This study reports the first complete mitochondrial genome of A. fruticosum and evaluates its comparative and phylogenetic relationships within Malvaceae. Methods The mitochondrial genome was assembled, annotated, and analyzed for genome composition, repetitive sequences, codon usage, predicted RNA-editing sites, nucleotide diversity, synonymous and nonsynonymous substitution rates, collinearity, and phylogenetic relationships inferred from 32 shared mitochondrial protein-coding genes across ten taxa. Results The mitogenome was assembled as a circular molecule of 826,313 bp, with a GC content of 44.94%, and contained 37 protein-coding genes, 3 rRNA genes, and 21 tRNA genes. Comparative analyses of five Malvaceae mitogenomes revealed conserved codon-usage patterns, with weak-to-moderate bias influenced by nucleotide composition and functional constraints, but substantial variation in repeat abundance and distribution. DeepredMT predicted 397 RNA-editing sites in A. fruticosum , fewer than in Tilia amurensis , Gossypium trilobum , and Hibiscus cannabinus , but slightly more than in Adansonia perrieri . Simple sequence repeats and short dispersed repeats predominated, whereas G. trilobum had the greatest proportion of long repeats and H. cannabinus the highest repeat density. Nucleotide-diversity hotspots were detected in rpl16 , rps3 , cox2 , and rpl2 , while most protein-coding genes had dN/dS values below 1. The elevated dN/dS signal in rps4 suggested accelerated evolution or relaxed functional constraint, warranting further investigation. Maximum-likelihood analysis recovered A. fruticosum (tribe Malveae) as sister to the sampled Hibiscus – Gossypium clade with strong support. Discussion This study presents the first mitochondrial genome of Abutilon , expanding mitogenomic resources for Malvaceae. The A. fruticosum mitogenome shows conserved gene content and codon usage, alongside lineage-specific variation in repeat organization, predicted RNA-editing sites, nucleotide diversity, and localized sequence divergence. The phylogenetic placement is consistent with the accepted classification of A. fruticosum in Malvoideae and illustrates the potential of mitogenomic data for systematic studies within Malvaceae, although broader taxon sampling is needed to test this placement. This mitogenome provides a resource for marker development, population-genetic studies, comparative mitogenomics, and phylogenetic research on Abutilon and related Malvaceae lineages.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tuberculosis caused by members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) poses significant threats to animal health, public health, and wildlife conservation. Mycobacterium orygis, an emerging MTBC member, remains poorly characterized with respect to its epidemiology and transmission dynamics among Indian wildlife and livestock. METHODS: Fifty-five necropsy tissue samples from 21 captive wild animals were subjected to mycobacterial culture and a panel of molecular diagnostic assays, including multiplex PCR, Xpert-Ultra, and Truenat MTB/Rif. Confirmed MTBC isolates were characterized by drug susceptibility testing (GenoType MTBDRplus) and spoligotyping. Six isolates were selected for whole-genome sequencing (WGS), and phylogenetic analyses were performed against publicly available reference genomes. RESULTS: Of 55 samples, 38 were MTBC-positive and 6 yielded nontuberculous mycobacteria. Drug susceptibility profiling revealed 28 pan-susceptible isolates, nine with isoniazid monoresistance, and one with rifampicin monoresistance. Spoligotyping classified 10 isolates as CAS1-Delhi, 27 as orphan lineages, and one remained unassigned. WGS of six isolates, representing diverse host species and tissue types, identified four as M. tuberculosis (CAS1-Delhi lineage). Notably, one orphan isolate from a blackbuck was reclassified as M. orygis. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that this M. orygis strain was genetically distinct from other Indian wildlife strains and most closely related to a human-derived isolate from Karnataka, suggesting cross-host genomic relatedness. The remaining isolates clustered with Indian and global reference genomes; one was closely related to cattle-derived strains, whereas four were more closely related to human-derived strains. Low pairwise SNP distances (0-78 SNPs) with strong bootstrap support indicated close genomic relatedness across host species and geographic regions. CONCLUSION: This study shows the MTBC genomic diversity among various hosts. The phylogenetic relationships suggest that there is genetic relatedness among host populations such as M. orygis in a captive Indian blackbuck, which was in human contact for a long time. The study demonstrates the importance of integrated One Health genomic surveillance of mycobacterial infections at the human-animal interface and calls for more extensive, epidemiologically linked studies to look for cross-host transmission pathways.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Rationale Point-of-care lung ultrasound is portable and radiation-free and could extend tuberculosis screening to settings without chest radiography, but no standardized criteria exist for interpreting it for tuberculosis. Objectives To develop and internally evaluate deep learning models that classify pulmonary tuberculosis from lung ultrasound images, alone and combined with routine clinical variables, and to derive an abbreviated scanning protocol. Methods In a prospective study in Kampala, Uganda (2023–2025), we enrolled people aged 13 years or older with microbiologically confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis, their household contacts, and symptomatic people with other respiratory conditions. One still frame from each of 12 lung ultrasound zones was analyzed with an attention-based multiple-instance learning network. We compared clinical-only (random forest), ultrasound-only, and combined models and derived a 6-zone protocol from training-set attention weights. Participants were allocated to training (n = 223), validation (n = 20), and held-out test (n = 73) sets. Results Of 318 enrolled participants, 316 were analyzed (118 with and 198 without tuberculosis). In the test set, areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve were 0.88 (95% confidence interval, 0.80–0.95) for the clinical-only model; 0.93 (0.86–0.97) and 0.95 (0.89–0.99) for the 12-zone ultrasound-only and combined models; and 0.91 (0.83–0.97) and 0.93 (0.86–0.99) for the corresponding 6-zone models. At 90% sensitivity, specificity was 82.2% (34.9–97.8) for the 12-zone combined model and 91.1% (25.0–98.0) for the 6-zone combined model. Point estimates for all 12-zone models and the 6-zone combined model met the 2025 World Health Organization minimum accuracy targets for a high-sensitivity screening test (≥90% sensitivity, ≥60% specificity). Conclusion Lung ultrasound analyzed with attention-based deep learning and combined with clinical variables showed high internal discrimination for pulmonary tuberculosis, and a simplified 6-zone protocol retained most of this performance. External validation in intended-use screening populations is needed.

research.abstract: Introduction The development of accurate and reliable diagnostic tools for tuberculosis remains a global health challenge. However, currently antibody-based assays lack sufficient sensitivity (30-40%). This study aimed to construct a multi-epitope fusion protein (Mtb6-Avi) and evaluate it for serological diagnosis and the assessment of radiographic severity. Methods The diagnostic antigen was designed based on 11 B-cell epitopes derived from six highly expressed Mycobacterium tuberculosis proteins. In this retrospective, single-center study, serum samples from 251 patients with pulmonary tuberculosis, 98 patients with non-TB pneumonia, and 20 healthy controls were analyzed by ELISA. A SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) analysis was used to explore the factors associated with radiographic severity. Results Serum Mtb6-Avi-binding antibody levels were significantly higher in patients with pulmonary tuberculosis than in patients with non-TB pneumonia and healthy controls (P < 0.001). The ROC curve yielded an AUC of 0.856 (95% CI, 0.819-0.893) with a sensitivity of 74.1% (95% CI, 68.2-79.4) and a specificity of 83.9% (95% CI, 76.0-90.0), indicating moderate diagnostic accuracy in this cohort. In a head-to-head comparison among 170 PTB patients without tumour or immune disorders, in whom both assays were performed, the sensitivity of the Mtb6-Avi assay was higher than that of one commercial TB antibody detection kit (74.1% vs 35.3%; McNemar's exact test, P < 0.001). In an exploratory SHAP analysis, C-reactive protein and the Mtb6-Avi-binding antibody had the highest mean absolute SHAP values among the predictors examined; these rankings describe associations within the model and require confirmation in independent cohorts. Conclusion In this retrospective cohort, the multi-epitope antigen was associated with higher sensitivity than one commercial serodiagnostic kit in the 170 patients with PTB in whom both assays had been performed; the comparison is restricted to a single comparator in a single subgroup and requires prospective confirmation. Antibody levels were associated with radiographic extent under two of the three severity definitions examined, but not with cavitary disease; they are therefore regarded as investigational markers rather than established indicators of pulmonary TB or of radiographic severity.

research.abstract: Tetrigidae is an early-branching family of Caelifera whose species live on damp ground, feed largely on mosses, algae and detritus, and often show wing and pronotum polymorphism. Which chemosensory and detoxification genes underlie this lifestyle is unknown. We generated an Oxford Nanopore PCR-cDNA transcriptome from a pooled sample of adult Hyboella guangxiensis (4.25 million full-length reads) and used it, together with protein homology, to filter the 17,996 machine-learning gene models of its chromosome-level genome to 15,338 supported genes without loss of BUSCO completeness. For nine families (OBP, CSP, IR, SNMP, P450, CCE, GST, UGT, ABC), full-length transcripts corrected 28 of 447 loci, including split and fused models, and brought protein lengths into agreement with orthologs of the sister species Bolivaritettix circocephalus (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.00066). Only 251 loci were supported by complete-ORF transcripts, and 101 had no full-length reads at all. Reconciliation of family phylogenies across eleven orthopteran genomes assigned 119 well-supported duplications to the Tetrigidae stem branch, dominated by P450 (42), UGT (27) and ABC (22) genes, and identified 63 homologous groups restricted to Tetrigidae. Five lineage-specific groups detected as transcripts in adults were validated at the genome level in four non-tetrigid outgroups: a CYP301A-like array, a Tetrigidae-specific UGT clade, two Tetrigidae-specific chemosensory proteins, a CYP9E2-like array and an esterase FE4-like array. Branch-site tests found episodic selection on some members of the UGT and CYP301A-like groups and in 7 of 28 recent paralog pairs, but not in the CYP9E2-like, FE4-like or CSP groups. These genes are candidates for the cuticular, chemosensory and dietary adaptations of pygmy grasshoppers to be tested with tissue-resolved data, whereas no family member could be linked to wing polymorphism.

research.abstract: Background Cardiac arrhythmias may remain unrecognized in adults with chronic disease. Established risk scores primarily address atrial fibrillation. Objective To develop and internally evaluate an electronic health record (EHR)–based machine-learning model to identify patients more likely to receive a documented cardiac arrhythmia diagnosis. Methods We retrospectively evaluated EHR data (2018–2025) from one healthcare organization among adults with type 2 diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic kidney disease, or coronary artery disease. Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost were compared. XGBoost was selected using internal validation, reduced to 30 features using Shapley additive explanations, and evaluated in a holdout set with data ending one day before the index date. Sensitivity analyses excluded information recorded within 30, 90, or 180 days before the index date. An atrial fibrillation/flutter-specific analysis compared XGBoost with CHARGE-AF and HARMS 2 -AF. Results Among 30,356 patients, 6,835 (22.5%) had a qualifying arrhythmia diagnosis. In 3,051 holdout patients, XGBoost achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.894 (95% CI 0.879–0.908) and an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.792 (95% CI 0.763–0.822). At a 0.5 threshold, sensitivity was 0.564, specificity 0.971, and precision 0.857. AUROC remained 0.896–0.897 across earlier cutoffs. In the common score-calculable atrial fibrillation/flutter subset ( n = 2,436), AUROCs were 0.883 for XGBoost, 0.712 for CHARGE-AF, and 0.554 for HARMS 2 -AF. Conclusions XGBoost demonstrated strong internal discrimination for documented arrhythmias. External validation and prospective evaluation are needed to assess generalizability and clinical utility.

research.abstract: Background: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) metrics, including time in range (TIR) and median glucose, guide therapeutic decisions in type 1 diabetes (T1D) but do not distinguish sustained from transient hyperglycaemia. We investigated the prevalence of short-lived hyperglycaemia (SLH), i.e. brief isolated hyperglycaemic episodes, and its contribution to CGM metrics in T1D children and adolescents. Methods: In this single-centre retrospective cohort study, T1D patients aged 6 months-20 years, enrolled in 2025-2026, with 5-minute CGM data, >=70% coverage and median glucose 6.1-9.4 mmol/L within a 45-day window were included. SLH were hyperglycaemic episodes lasting 10-60 minutes surrounded by normoglycaemia, classified by onset as daytime or night-time. Their contribution to CGM metrics was estimated by replacing SLH with plausible trajectories; sensitivity analyses varied construction parameters. Findings: Among 135 participants, 2,874 of 15,556 hyperglycaemic episodes (18.5%) met daytime SLH criteria (median 19.0 per participant). Removing SLH increased daytime TIR by 1.74 percentage points (95% CI 1.59-1.89) and reduced daytime median glucose by 0.18 mmol/L (95% CI 0.17-0.20). Whole-day effects were modest, but local impact was substantially greater: at maximal divergence, glucose profiles differed by 1.30 mmol/L (95% CI 1.21-1.38), around meals. Patients with near-identical conventional metrics could show markedly different SLH frequency. Interpretation: SLH are common in this paediatric T1D cohort and alter routinely reported CGM metrics: modest whole-day effect contrasts with a substantially greater impact at specific times of day. Distinguishing transient from sustained hyperglycaemia provides clinically relevant information beyond aggregate metrics and may guide behavioural or educational interventions rather than insulin intensification.
