research.abstract: Abstract Whole-blood transcriptomic signatures are widely proposed for tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis, but reported performance often degrades when applied to new populations. We attempt to identify how much of this can be attributed to variables like model choice, panels, tasks and cohorts. We evaluated three trained classifiers (logistic regression, random forest and a multilayer perceptron) alongside two untrained scores (singscore and directional gene average). These were applied to four published panels: Kaforou (task-specific), Zak16, Sweeney3 and Berry86. Two panels were derived internally and benchmarked: Nat(mRMR), and Nat. They were compared with 50 size-matched random panels for control and significance testing. The analysis used 952 unique samples from 10 public GEO series across three diagnostic tasks, with rotating leave-one-cohort-out (LOCO) validation. Two independent cohorts, GSE144127 active tuberculosis (ATB) vs other disease (OD) and GSE152218 (ATB vs latent tuberculosis (LTB)), served as external validation; in these, panels were compared with Holm-adjusted paired DeLong tests. Generalisability was strongly task-dependent: ATB vs LTB achieved excellent cross-cohort generalisation, consistent with previous reports. However, for ATB vs LTB random panels performed comparably, with performance only diverging when panel sizes shrank, indicating that the task itself is simpler than the others. ATB vs OD exhibited lower performance depending on the panel chosen (AUCs of 0.40-0.94; median 0.75), with the mRMR-derived panel accounting for the lower bound and failing to exceed random panels in any fold. LTB vs control (CON) showed no discernible signal across panels, models and random controls (AUC 0.39-0.78; median 0.57). Model architecture exerted minimal influence compared to the underlying biological signal, with an exception for the ATB vs OD task. Both of the final locked panels were then tested on fully independent cohorts (AUC 0.86 and 0.96). There was no significant difference between these and the published panels post Holm adjustment. An additional test on sarcoidosis had failure across all panels.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Marine sponges (phylum Porifera) are a highly diverse and polymorphic group of marine invertebrates whose taxonomic delimitation is often challenging due to high intraspecific variability and the scarcity of diagnostic morphological characters. Their close association with microbial symbionts also makes them an important source of secondary metabolites, some of which may contribute to sponge colouration. Here, we use morphological characters, molecular phylogenetic markers, and 16S metabarcoding of the symbiont community to understand speciation in a common Mediterranean sponge lineage. We collected 43 specimens of the genus Suberites from the Mediterranean Sea and the North and South Atlantic Oceans, between 55– 150 m depths, and sequenced two barcoding genes, cytochrome c oxidase I and 28S rDNA, as well as studied their spicular complements. We identified five closely-related species: S. domuncula , S. ficus/pagurorum , S. dandelenae , S. ambulodomus , and a new species of Suberites from the Balearic Islands, Suberites sp. nov. The latter represents a potential new pseudo-cryptic species closely related to S. domuncula , because of their strong morphological and molecular affinities. These results provide valuable insights into species boundaries and evolutionary relationships within the genus Suberites and support a role for the microbiome in sponge colouration.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Cultivated peanut ( Arachis hypogaea L.) is an allotetraploid crop (2n = 4x = 40) with an AABB genome that preserves extensive synteny between its two subgenomes. This characteristic, along with the availability of multiple genomic resources, provides a valuable framework for the comprehensive characterization of gene families and for inferring their evolutionary dynamics. Here we report a genome-wide analysis of the Dof transcription factor family in peanut (AhyDof), including phylogenetic inferences, gene structures, chromosomal locations, patterns of gene duplication, and expression analysis. Results ​A total of 66 non-redundant Dof genes (AhyDofs) were identified and unevenly distributed across the A and B subgenom​es. Comparative analyses revealed extensive conservation of gene structure, protein motifs, and chromosomal localization among homeologous genes inherited from the diploid progenitors, indicating that allopolyploidization contributed to family expansion while having a limited impact on gene diversification. Phylogenetic analyses placed AhyDofs within the four major angiosperm Dof lineages, supporting the evolutionary conservation of this family across flowering plants. Synteny analyses further identified chromosomal rearrangements and tandem duplication events contributing to the current composition of the AhyDof repertoire. Most notably, we discovered a novel group of six Dof genes associated with previously undescribed Pack-MULE transposons, designated AMuD, providing the first evidence of Pack-MULE-mediated transduplication in the genus Arachis . Structural and phylogenetic analyses suggested that these elements originated from non-autonomous MULEs and captured an ancestral Dof gene related to AhyDof-15.3. The dN/dS rate analysis suggested that transduplicated genes may have evolved under selective constraint, potentially indicating that functional constraints were maintained after mobilization. Comparative genomic analyses, PCR assays across diploid species, and Oxford Nanopore sequencing data suggested that AMuD elements originated within the B–F–K lineage of section Arachis and were maintained during peanut domestication and diversification. Promoter analyses revealed distinct cis-regulatory architectures among AMuD-derived genes, while transcriptomic data demonstrated their transcriptional activity, particularly in reproductive tissues. Conclusions The evolution of the peanut Dof repertoire in peanut was shaped by multiple mechanisms, including polyploidization, chromosomal rearrangements, tandem duplication, and lineage-specific Pack-MULE-mediated transduplication. The discovery of AMuD elements reveals a previously undescribed mechanism contributing to the diversification of regulatory genes in Arachis and provides new insights into the evolutionary dynamics of plant transcription factor families.

research.abstract: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. Here, we present BEAGLE 4.1, a high-performance library for statistical phylogenetics that incorporates new algorithms to evaluate these gradients on phylogenetic trees. We also provide new hardware implementations for both likelihoods and gradients supporting ARM NEON intrinsics and optimized matrix multiplication units -- called tensor cores -- on NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs). We benchmark the performance scaling of the library across a number of patterns and taxa on multi-core CPUs and GPUs, and compare the speedup afforded by NVIDIA and AMD GPUs as well as performance scaling with an increasing number of GPUs. We show that multi-core CPU implementations provide up to a fourfold speedup over single-threaded CPU implementations and up to an tenfold speedup for nucleotide and codon models, respectively, with performance generally improving as the number of taxa and site patterns increases. GPUs outperform multi-threaded CPU implementations for a realistic number of patterns, even for nucleotide models with a small state-space size of 4, while for codon models they provide substantially higher performance gains even for a single pattern or four taxa. Tensor cores on GPUs provide up to 2-fold speedup relative to standard CUDA cores for codon models. Using NEON instructions on ARM CPUs affords up to a $\sim 1.3$-fold speedup over non-SIMD implementation with the speedup going down to 1.1-fold at 8 CPU threads. We provide these new algorithms to evaluate the gradient and efficient hardware implementations for both likelihood and gradient calculations through BEAGLE 4.1, such that they can be readily integrated into phylogenetic software packages.

research.abstract: Abstract Meiotic recombination ensures proper chromosome segregation and generates genetic variation among offspring. Recombination rates vary across taxa, with social Hymenoptera exhibiting some of the highest rates reported among multicellular animals, yet it remains an open question how such extreme recombination rates shape genome evolution. Here, we present a high-density linkage map for the California harvester ant Pogonomyrmex californicus and report an average genome-wide recombination rate of 14.73 cM/Mb, the highest documented for an ant to date. Recombination was strongly suppressed in gene-poor, repeat-rich regions and was positively associated with nucleotide diversity and genomic GC content. At the gene level, recombination rate was not associated with nonsynonymous substitution rate ( d N ) and showed no robust association with ω ( d N /d S ), providing little evidence that variation in local recombination rate is associated with detectable differences in selection efficacy among protein-coding genes. In contrast, synonymous substitution rate ( d S ) declined with recombination rate, whereas observed GC content at third codon positions (GC3) and inferred equilibrium GC content (GC3*) increased. These relationships persisted after accounting for gene-body methylation, which itself was negatively associated with recombination rate. Our results show that exceptionally high recombination rates are associated with variation in nucleotide diversity and base composition, with clear signatures of GC-biased sequence evolution.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Animal species differ dramatically in their overall size, yet the mechanisms underlying these differences are poorly understood. The Hippo pathway, first discovered in Drosophila , and widely conserved in mammals, regulates the nuclear levels of YAP1, a transcriptional co-activator that enhances the expression of growth-promoting genes. While experimental manipulations of this pathway elicit dramatic effects on tissue growth and organ size, it is not known whether, and to what extent, evolutionary divergence of this pathway has contributed to size differences across animals. Here we show that although YAP1 protein sequence is highly conserved between diverse mammals such as humans, elephants and blue whales, it diverges considerably among rodent species. While the human YAP1 protein is very similar to that of the largest rodent, the capybara Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris , those of smaller rodents such as the mouse Mus musculus and the vole Microtus oregoni show considerable divergence. An increased ratio of non-synonymous versus synonymous substitutions (dN/dS) in clades of small rodents compared to the background is indicative of relaxed constraint in these lineages, suggesting relative positive selection. When expressed in the developing Drosophila wing, capybara YAP1 was more potent at promoting growth than that of the mouse or vole. Following transfection into mammalian cells, capybara YAP1 is more effective at promoting expression of a reporter gene than either mouse or vole YAP1. Thus, by combining computational and experimental approaches, we show that evolutionarily divergent coding-region changes in YAP1 have likely contributed to the evolution of smaller body size in clades of rodents.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Clp proteases are central to bacterial proteostasis, yet our biochemical understanding of actinobacterial Clp enzymes derives almost entirely from mycobacteria, where their essentiality complicates efforts to understand their physiological behavior. Here, we reconstitute and biochemically characterize the ClpCP1P2 protease from Corynebacterium glutamicum , a genetically tractable actinobacterium in which clpC and clpX are non-essential. We find that, as in Mycobacterium tuberculosis , ClpP1 and ClpP2 are individually inactive and form an active peptidase only when stabilized by ATP-bound ClpC or acyldepsipeptide antibiotics, with further stimulation by N-blocked peptide agonists. However, C. glutamicum ClpCP1P2 exhibits faster kinetics and greater conformational stability than its mycobacterial orthologs, proteolyzing full-length substrates rapidly without requiring peptide agonists. We additionally show that the anti-mycobacterial antibiotics rufomycin and cyclomarin A bind the C. glutamicum ClpC N-terminal domain, exert substrate-specific effects on proteolysis, and impair C. glutamicum growth. The ability of these compounds to elicit toxicity through a non-essential target suggests that they act via gain-of-function dysregulation rather than simple inhibition. Together, our results validate C. glutamicum as a tractable model for interrogating Actinomycetota Clp proteases. IMPORTANCE Mycobacterium tuberculosis remains one of the world’s deadliest bacterial pathogens and its Clp proteases are promising targets for new antibiotics. However, because these enzymes are essential in mycobacteria, it is difficult to study their physiological roles. Here, we show that the Clp protease of Corynebacterium glutamicum , a non-pathogenic relative in which the unfoldase ClpC is dispensable, shares the core assembly and regulatory features of its mycobacterial counterpart while being more stable and catalytically faster. Anti-mycobacterial ClpC-targeting antibiotics also act on this system, supporting a model in which they cause protease dysregulation rather than simple inhibition. These findings establish a genetically tractable model for dissecting actinobacterial Clp protease mechanisms and antibiotic action. They may also inform strategies for engineering regulated protein degradation in C. glutamicum , an important industrial microbe.

research.abstract: Cough drives respiratory pathogen transmission, yet how microorganisms directly engage host nociceptive neurons to trigger cough is largely unknown. We previously demonstrated that Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) glycolipid sulfolipid-1 activates neurons and induces cough. Here we identify a phenolic glycolipid (PGL) produced by the hypertransmissible Mtb strain HN878 as an additional activator of mouse and human nociceptive neurons, and we show that purified PGL is sufficient to induce cough in guinea pigs. Together, PGL and sulfolipid-1 elicit greater neuronal activation than either glycolipid alone. By synthesizing various PGL analogues, we show that neuroactivity depends on saccharide chain length and structure. Mechanistically, neurons release ATP extracellularly following PGL stimulation, which engages neuronal P2X3 purinergic receptors. This effect is blocked by a P2X3 antagonist, gefapixant. These findings reveal a neuronal activation pathway co-opted by certain Mtb strains to induce cough and suggest inhibition of purinergic signalling as a potential strategy to block airborne spread of Mtb.

research.abstract: Abstract Eco-evolutionary feedbacks are typically thought to require an ecological change driving Darwinian selection. However, ecology can drive other evolutionary mechanisms too. In many microbial species mutation rates are elevated at low population density, mediated by nutrient availability and reactive oxygen species (ROS). These findings from monoculture populations led us to hypothesise that the presence and density of a cohabiting species will also affect mutation rates. Using Escherichia coli as a focal species we explore the mutational effects on both parties of co-culture with either Enterococcus faecalis or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. These species co-occur in multiple clinical settings and have different abilities to degrade ROS. In both co-culture systems we find evidence that the presence of a stronger ROS degrader reduces mutation rates in the weaker ROS degrading species. At the same time increasing population density of the weaker ROS degrader increases mutation rates in the stronger ROS degrading species. Simultaneous mutation rate estimation in co-cultured species raises multiple experimental challenges addressed here. Despite these challenges, we find evidence for a novel form of eco-evo feedback in which the environment shapes the supply of mutational variation to the population. This in turn feeds back to alter the chance of evolutionary rescue for one species or another during a subsequent environmental change. Such effects potentially matter not only for our fundamental understanding of the interplay between ecology and evolution, but for the treatment of polymicrobial infections in which rates of resistance evolution may be altered by the cross-species mutational effects of cohabiting species.

research.abstract: Abstract Codon-based maximum likelihood models are the workhorse of molecular selection analysis, yet standard workflows assume that the input sequence alignment and phylogenetic tree are known without error. In practice, heuristic aligners ignore the genetic code and phylogeny, which packs non-homologous codons into shared columns across insertion-deletion loops and inflates gene-wide false-positive rates above 80%. This sequential division of labor is statistically suboptimal and computationally wasteful. Here, we present WALRUS ( W heatstone A lignment and L ikelihood R ate U nification for S election), a unified engine in H y P hy 3 ( https://github.com/veg/hyphy-3 ) that maps unaligned coding sequences to a coordinate-consistent selection atlas in one run. From a single Inside–Outside likelihood table, the pipeline repairs reading frames, co-estimates a codon alignment and Ohmic reticulate network, models directional base-composition drift, and evaluates eight selection tests (BUSTED-E, aBSREL, RELAX, FEL, dFEL, MEME, Contrast-FEL, and PRIME). Across 10,020 simulated alignments, WALRUS recovers 94.6% of true columns on the 800 INDELible replicates and cuts indel-driven false positives from 44.7%– 58.1% to 4.4% under BUSTED (21.1%– 21.4% to 1.4% under BUSTED-E). Under Zipfian indel saturation, false positives drop four-fold (33.3%– 83.3% to 17.0%– 20.5%), while 11, 190 avian orthogroup runs execute 6.6–35.8-fold faster and cut housekeeping false positives 13-fold (28-fold on ultraconserved genes) proteome-wide.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Whole-genome sequencing of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) commonly relies on culture-derived isolates, potentially altering the bacterial populations represented. Direct sputum whole-genome sequencing (dsWGS) may better capture lineage composition and within-host variant diversity. Methods We compared targeted-enrichment dsWGS with WGS of matched culture-derived isolates from participants initiating treatment for rifampicin-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis in Worcester, South Africa. We assessed sequencing performance, technical reproducibility, sputum-sampling variability, lineage and variant concordance, and resistance-associated variation, and explored associations with baseline clinical characteristics and treatment response. Results Of 218 clinical dsWGS reactions, 139 passed sequencing quality criteria, yielding 113 eligible baseline sputum–culture pairs. Mixed-lineage infection was detected in 72/113 (63.7%) sputum specimens versus 7/113 (6.2%) matched cultures; 66/113 (58.4%) pairs showed reduced lineage diversity following culture. Permutation analysis indicated preferential retention of Lineage 2 and depletion of Lineage 3 after culture. Technical replicates preserved dominant phylotype assignments (median SNP Jaccard similarity 0.863), while independently collected sputum specimens showed greater variability. Among 38 concordant single-lineage pairs, 35,540/38,311 (92.8%) pair-specific variant observations were shared after filtering and raw-read recovery, while 2,497 (6.5%) were sputum-unique and 274 (0.7%) culture-unique. Discordance was concentrated among variable variants; 88.0% of shared variants variable in at least one specimen had higher allele frequencies in culture. No sputum-unique WHO Grade 1 or 2 resistance-associated mutations were identified in the strain-controlled subset, whereas eight mixed-lineage sputum samples versus three matched cultures harboured such mutations. Higher baseline low-frequency variant burden showed non-significant trends towards delayed culture conversion (log-rank p=0.144) and unfavourable treatment outcomes (log-rank p=0.400). Conclusions Direct-sputum WGS revealed M. tuberculosis lineage and low-frequency variant diversity that was not fully represented by matched culture-derived genomes, despite high overall genomic concordance. These findings highlight the complementary value of direct-sputum sequencing for characterising within-host diversity, while suggesting that the representation of bacterial populations following culture may vary across epidemiological settings. Further research is needed to improve the accuracy of minority-variant detection and establish the clinical relevance of diversity measured directly from sputum.

research.abstract: Abstract Orthology inference is foundational for comparative genomics, enabling the reconstruction of phylogenetic relationships and transfer of biological knowledge between species. Methods often infer different orthogroups and orthologous relationships, making robust benchmarking essential for evaluating their accuracy. Existing resources such as the Quest for Orthologs benchmark service and OrthoBench provide valuable benchmarks grounded in real biological data and expert curation. However, the true evolutionary histories in all of these benchmarks are unknown, and therefore the true accuracy of orthology inference methods is unknown. Simulations provide an approach to evaluate accuracy where the complete ground truth is known. However, simulations are only useful for benchmarking if they realistically reflect empirical data. Here, we introduce OrthoSimulator, a Python package for generating realistic, empirically calibrated benchmark datasets with known orthogroups, orthologous relationships, gene trees, and evolutionary events. We demonstrate its utility by benchmarking widely used orthology inference methods across simulations calibrated from multiple methods and empirical datasets. We show that method-to-method variability in ortholog inference accuracy is robust to variation in simulation parameters. We further provide a detailed evaluation of ortholog inference accuracy through independent cross-validation, and show that OrthoFinder is the most accurate of the four methods tested. OrthoSimulator is freely available at https://github.com/lauriebelch/OrthoSimulator . Significance Statement Comparative genomics relies on orthology, the identification of genes that descend from a single gene in a common ancestor. Many methods infer orthologs, and they often disagree, but their true accuracy is hard to measure because the true history of real genes is never known. We present OrthoSimulator, which learns from real genomes to simulate realistic gene families whose full history is recorded. The simulations complement existing benchmarks built from real genes by adding complete ground truth. We use them to compare four widely used methods and to measure errors that cannot be seen in real data, and the simulated genomes can test any method that reconstructs gene family evolution.

research.abstract: Abstract Introduction Type 2 diabetes can impair productivity during working age (20–69 years), causing substantial economic burden at individual and at population level. We aimed to estimate age- and sex-specific productivity-adjusted life years (PALYs) lost due to type 2 diabetes by socioeconomic position (SEP) between 2022 and 2060 in Germany. Methods We used an established projection model and nationally representative, publicly available German data to estimate age- and sex-specific PALYs lost due to type 2 diabetes by SEP among working-age adults, accounting for future incidence trends. PALYs lost were calculated as the sum of years of life lost (YLL) and years of productivity lost (YPL) due to reduced labour force participation, presenteeism, and absenteeism, using SEP-specific estimates from representative studies. Results Productivity losses were highest among persons with low SEP, followed by those with medium and high SEP. In 2022, 20-year-old men with type 2 diabetes and low, medium, and high SEP were projected to lose 11.32 PALYs (95% confidence interval (CI) 7.99–14.56), 8.19 PALYs (95% CI 6.01–10.33), and 3.78 PALYs (95% CI 0.89–6.72), respectively, by age 69 compared with men without type 2 diabetes, mainly driven by YPL. A comparable socioeconomic gradient was observed among women and remained largely unchanged until 2060. At the population level, an estimated 9.5 million PALYs (95% CI 6.42–12.58) were lost due to type 2 diabetes in 2022 in both sexes. This number is projected to increase to 9.5–13.5 million by 2060, mainly driven by the projected increase in the number of persons with type 2 diabetes. Conclusion Type 2 diabetes-related productivity losses were shaped by SEP, sex and the future number of persons with the disease. PALYs lost declined with age and were predominantly driven by YPL.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Dosing guidance for children with leprosy remains operationally challenging. For children under 10 years of age, current WHO recommendations rely on mg/kg dosing of the three separate components of leprosy multidrug therapy, which are difficult to implement in routine care and may result in inconsistent drug exposures. Weight-banded dosing offers a pragmatic alternative that better aligns with pharmacokinetic principles and existing drug formulations. Methodology A pharmacokinetic simulation study was conducted to develop harmonized weight-banded dosing regimens for rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone in children aged 2 to 10 years. Using the WHO dosing tool, drug exposures across harmonized weight bands were simulated and adult-equivalent systemic exposure (80–125% of adult area under the concentration–time curve) targeted. Predicted exposures were contextualized against safety reference regimens used in tuberculosis meningitis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, and leprosy. An iterative review process involving the WHO Technical Working Group on leprosy in children ensured clinical and operational feasibility. Results Proposed weight-banded multidrug therapy regimens achieved adult-equivalent exposures across most weight bands. Predicted exposures modestly exceeded 125% of adult levels at the lower end of selected weight bands but remained well below safety benchmarks, namely exposures associated with daily rifampicin therapy for tuberculosis meningitis and clofazimine regimens for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. Dapsone exposures were comparable to those achieved with current leprosy dosing. The existing 10–14-year-old child MDT blister pack could be used without modification in children weighing 25–39.9 kg and with limited tablet or gel capsule removal in children weighing 6–24.9 kg. Conclusions A harmonized weight-banded dosing strategy was developed that enables effective, practical dosing of leprosy multidrug therapy in children under 10 years using existing free-of-charge blister packs provided through WHO. This approach improves dosing consistency, supports programmatic implementation, and provides a rational interim solution while child-friendly formulations are being developed. Author Summary Leprosy continues to affect children in many low-resource settings, yet guidance on how to dose treatment in younger children remains limited. Current recommendations often require clinicians to calculate mg/kg doses, which can be difficult in practice and may not match the oral formulations that are available. In this study, we used computer-based simulations to develop a simplified dosing approach for the three drugs used to treat leprosy. We showed that grouping children into weight bands, rather than calculating individual doses, can achieve drug exposures similar to those seen in adults, where treatment is known to be effective. Importantly, we found that these doses can be delivered using existing pre-packed treatment kits by removing selected dose units, making this approach practical in routine care. This work provides a more straightforward and reliable way to treat children with leprosy, reducing the burden on clinicians and improving access to treatment. However, challenges remain, including the lack of child-friendly formulations and limited data on how these drugs behave in children. Further studies are needed to improve treatment for this vulnerable population.

research.abstract: Abstract Bacteria engage in many cooperative behaviours which provide benefits to other cells in the population. Lab experiments have suggested that these costly behaviours can be favoured by kin selection due to the benefits they provide to closely related cells. However, we know much less about the role of kin selection in natural populations. Here, we used two complementary methods to measure and compare kin selected signatures of cooperation in 19 species of bacteria found in the guts of honey bees. We used bioinformatic tools to count the number (and proportion) of genes for cooperative traits in a genome, and used molecular population genetics to measure how natural selection is acting on those genes. We found evidence for a consistent signature of kin selection for cooperation on genes controlling cooperative traits across species. Genes for cooperative traits had more non-synonymous relative to synonymous polymorphism than genes for private traits, had more protein-changing mutations and more codons under positive selection, and were lost more often. From this signature, we estimate an average relatedness of 0.73 between interacting cells. However, we found no evidence supporting the prediction that this signature varies with relatedness estimated from metagenomes. These patterns suggest that whilst genes for cooperative traits are undergoing kin selection in natural populations, there may be other factors influencing how the action of kin selection varies across species. Impact Statement Bacteria cooperate by secreting molecules that benefit other cells, such as enzymes that break down food and molecules that take up iron. Kin selection theory predicts that genes for these cooperative traits are under weaker selection than genes for private traits, which benefit only the cell that makes them. We tested this prediction across 19 species of bacteria from the honey bee gut. As predicted, we found that genes for cooperative traits had more non-synonymous relative to synonymous polymorphism than those for private traits. Between strains of the same species, genes for cooperative traits had more protein-changing mutations and more positively selected codons, and were lost more often. However, these differences did not vary across species with relatedness estimated from metagenomes. One possible reason is that bacteria interact in small patches of the gut, so our whole-gut metagenomic estimates of relatedness may not be accurate.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Synonymous codon usage bias (CUB) provides a complementary perspective on molecular variation, but its relationship with morphological diversity in rapidly radiating plant lineages remains poorly understood. We investigated this relationship in Thelypteridaceae by integrating chloroplast phylogenomics, codon usage analyses, and published descriptions of lamina base architecture. A phylogeny based on 31 shared protein‐coding genes provided the evolutionary framework for 37 plastome accessions, including two outgroups. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) revealed three major codon usage groupings (Types A–C) that partly differed from the chloroplast phylogeny, with Types A and C corresponding descriptively to contrasting lamina base forms. A focused comparison of 27 accessions and eight genes retained this Type A–Type C separation. Although ENC, PR2, and neutrality plots showed broadly similar overall patterns between the types, gene‐wise analyses highlighted ndhJ, psaA, and psbD, and protein‐guided codon alignments reproduced their type‐specific synonymous third‐position counts. These complementary observations support a relationship between chloroplast codon usage variation and frond architecture in the sampled taxa. They identify candidate photosynthesis‐related loci and provide a basis for testing the evolutionary and functional processes underlying this relationship.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Childhood respiratory infectious deaths are partitioned across four Global Burden of Disease cause modules—26 etiological attributions within lower respiratory infections, tuberculosis, COVID-19, and whooping cough—never jointly reported. Whether the structure of this combined mortality spectrum has changed over time, and with what implications for intervention design, has not been quantified. We assembled and analyzed the integrated spectrum for children and adolescents aged 0– 19 years, 1990–2023. Methods We integrated Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 (release v8352) estimates into a 29-node spectrum—26 lower respiratory infection etiologies plus tuberculosis, COVID-19, and pertussis— globally and across seven super-regions, with uncertainty propagated by summing bounds. We computed Shannon diversity, Herfindahl concentration, and effective cause counts; phenotyped pandemic-window collapse and rebound per cause; linked pathogen shares to WHO/UNICEF vaccine coverage; and mapped geographic concentration in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Segmented (joinpoint) log-linear models with breakpoints selected by the Bayesian information criterion were fitted to annual totals, Shannon diversity and leading pathogen shares. Results In 2023 the 29 causes jointly accounted for 965,330 deaths (95% uncertainty interval [UI] 680,096–1,342,437). Shannon diversity rose from 2.336 to 2.711 (+16.1%) between 1990 and 2023; the effective number of causes nearly doubled (5.57 to 9.94), inversely coupled to total deaths (Spearman ρ = −0.997). Whooping cough ranked second (112,954 deaths; 95% UI 64,576–185,708; 11.7%) and showed the spectrum’s only rebound above 100% (−57.4% collapse, +111.0% rebound). Tuberculosis ranked third (87,764; 57,779–124,912; 9.1%) with the highest concentration in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia (87.1%). COVID-19 entered at rank five (52,899; 47,275–59,183; 5.5%). Nineteen of 29 causes exceeded the poverty-lock threshold (>80.59% of deaths in sub-Saharan Africa plus South Asia). Joinpoint analysis placed breakpoints in total deaths at 2011, 2018 and 2021—the decline slowed from −3.4% to −2.3% per year after 2011, steepened to −7.1% per year in 2018–2021 and rebounded +4.5% per year in 2021–2023—while diversification accelerated to +1.18% per year in 2013–2020; all six leading pathogen shares carried a pandemic-window breakpoint at 2019 and 2021 (S. pneumoniae at 2018 and 2021). Conclusions Childhood respiratory infectious mortality has become more diverse and more concentrated in poverty as it has declined. Single-pathogen interventions now address a shrinking share; the spectrum’s structure argues for platform interventions—oxygen, antimicrobial access, referral—tailored jointly by age and geography, implying that pathogen-specific strategies alone cannot finish the remaining mortality agenda.

research.abstract: BackgroundThe American Heart Association defined Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) syndrome in 2023. Census-tract studies often examined one condition without spatial modeling. It is unclear where combined Stage 1-2 burden concentrates and how it relates to aging, environment, and socioeconomic conditions. MethodsWe built a CKM burden index for 70,336 tracts from five CDC PLACES crude prevalences (obesity, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, chronic kidney disease) and compared it with NHANES 2017-2020. In 69,530 contiguous-U.S. tracts, we fit Bayesian spatial (BYM2) models with demographic, socioeconomic, and environmental predictors and aging x environment interactions, plus descriptive machine learning. The primary model excluded behavioral measures sharing the outcomes BRFSS source; a second added them. Credible intervals (CrIs) are conditional on PLACES estimates. ResultsAgreement with NHANES was modest. Burden clustered spatially (Morans I = 0.657) and highest in the South. Behavioral measures had the largest machine-learning importance (52.6%), partly from shared sourcing. Each percentage-point increase in adults [≥]65 years was associated with 0.112 units higher burden (95% CrI 0.111-0.113) outside low-income, low-access (LILA) tracts. LILA tracts had 0.10-0.14 units higher burden from the 25th aging percentile but not consistently in the youngest decile. Aging and socioeconomic associations held across sensitivity analyses. The primary models residual Southern excess approached zero after adding behavioral measures, which may reflect shared measurement, real differences in these behaviors, or both. ConclusionsCKM burden is spatially clustered and highest in the South. LILA tracts had modestly higher burden above the youngest tracts. These cross-sectional estimates support area-level surveillance and needs assessment. research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Variation in the gut microbiome composition has been associated with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) in case-control designs. We aimed to investigate associations with incident ASCVD events applying a prospective design to reduce the impact of reverse causality. Methods We assessed associations between gut microbiome features measured by shotgun metagenomic sequencing and incident total ASCVD, ischemic heart disease (IHD) and ischemic stroke, including fatal and non-fatal events as defined by registry follow-up in 17,216 participants from three Swedish population-based cohorts (SCAPIS, SIMPLER, and MOS). Results from Cox proportional hazards regression models adjusted for demographic, and lifestyle factors, medication, and prevalent diabetes were combined across cohorts using a fixed-effect meta-analysis accounting for multiple testing. Associations were tested for replication in HUNT and FINRISK. Results During a median of 6-8 y follow-up, 769 incident ASCVD events occurred. Species diversity was inversely associated with ASCVD and IHD, with a hazard ratio for IHD of 0.86 per SD increase in species richness (95% CI: 0.79-0.95). Sixty-eight common species (i.e., present in ≥30% individuals) were associated with incident IHD after adjusting for sex and birth country, but only eight remained in fully adjusted models, including Ruminococcus_B gnavus . Among others, inverse associations were observed for SFEL01 sp004557245 and Fimadaptatus sp900553645 from Christensenellales , an order in which butyrate production has been reported. Streptococcus mutans and Limosilactobacillus fermentum, oral-associated species previously associated with coronary atherosclerosis, were associated with a higher risk of incident IHD, which remained after adjustment for dental health. Replication analysis in the HUNT study supported the finding for S. mutans . No associations were observed with ischemic stroke. Conclusions Gut species diversity and specific species abundance were associated with incident IHD, providing evidence supporting a protective role of two Christensenellales species and an adverse role of oral species and R. gnavus in the development of IHD.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Current projections of the prevalence and number of persons with type 2 diabetes by socioeconomic position (SEP) are lacking for Germany. This study aims to project age-specific type 2 diabetes prevalence in Germany by sex and SEP between 2022 and 2060. Methods We used a partial differential equation (PDE) based on the illness-death model to project age-specific type 2 diabetes prevalence by sex and SEP between 2022 and 2060. The PDE describes the relationship between prevalence, incidence, all-cause mortality and the mortality rate ratio (MRR) of individuals with vs. without type2 diabetes considering age, calendar year and SEP. SEP was measured by quintiles of the German Index of Socioeconomic Deprivation (GISD). Baseline prevalence, incidence, and MRR in 2022 were derived from statutory health insurance data (∼85% of the German population). Projected prevalence was multiplied by population projections from the German Federal Statistical Office to estimate the number of persons with diabetes. Results Type 2 diabetes prevalence increases with age, peaking between 80 and 90 years. Between 2022 and 2060, age-specific prevalence is projected to increase for both sexes across all SEP groups. SEP-related disparities persisted with largest differences between the highest (5th GISD quintile) and lowest (1st GISD quintile) SEP group. The number of persons with type 2 diabetes is projected to rise from 8.4 million in 2022 to between 11.2 and 19.2 million in 2060. Conclusions Between 2022 and 2060, age-specific type 2 diabetes prevalence is projected to increase with increasing socioeconomic inequalities.

research.abstract: SUMMARY Background Swab-based molecular testing for tuberculosis (TB) could provide a near point-of-care (nPOC) diagnostic for children. We evaluated the accuracy of two swab-based nPOC platforms to detect pediatric pulmonary TB. Methods We prospectively enrolled children under 15 years with presumptive TB in Uganda and South Africa. They completed TB evaluation including sputum molecular testing and culture. Two tongue swabs were collected and tested with MiniDock MTB (Pluslife Biotech, China) and Truenat MTB Ultima (Molbio Diagnostics, India), and one swab was dipped in sputum for testing with MiniDock MTB. We calculated the sensitivity and specificity of each index test against a culture-based standard and compared them with sputum molecular testing and smear microscopy. Findings We included 335 children, among whom median age was 3 years (IQR 1-6), 53% were female, 11% were living with HIV, and 16% had microbiologically confirmed TB. Tongue swabs were collected in all children, with invalid test rates of less than 3%. Against a culture-based standard, the sensitivities of tongue swab MiniDock MTB and MTB Ultima were 50% (95% CI 33.4-66.6) and 50% (95% CI 28.2-71.8), respectively, and specificities were ≥98% for both. Sputum swab MiniDock MTB had similar sensitivity to sputum Xpert Ultra (85.7% vs. 75.0%, p=0.45), but substantially higher sensitivity than tongue swab MiniDock MTB (+23.1%, p=0.03) and sputum smear microscopy (+46.4%, p<0.001). Interpretation Sputum swab testing had similar accuracy to sputum Xpert Ultra in children. Tongue swab testing had moderate accuracy, and has value to identify microbiologically confirmed cases when sputum is not available. Funding National Institutes of Health, United States Department of State Bureau of Global Health Security and Diplomacy, and South African Medical Research Council RESEARCH IN CONTEXT Evidence before this study We evaluated the literature from October 2021 to October 2026 for studies in any language on oral swab molecular testing for M. tuberculosis (MTB). We included diagnostic accuracy studies and excluded work on extrapulmonary TB, screening and early assay development, and searched PubMed and Google Scholar with the terms “swab” AND “tuberculosis” AND “diagnosis.” Manual quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) testing on tongue swabs has high accuracy to detect pulmonary TB in adults (80-93% sensitive and >98% specificity), with similar accuracy to sputum samples. Translation to semi-automated PCR assays such as Xpert Ultra have had high specificity but variable sensitivity (59-76%). Newer assays have been developed that are designed specifically for swab testing, and are small, portable, and can be used near the point-of-care (nPOC). Studies in adults have found that nPOC tongue swab testing is feasible, sensitive (75-86%), and specific (>96%). Testing can also be performed by dipping a swab in sputum, offering higher accuracy than tongue swabs and similar performance to sputum Xpert Ultra. However, the evidence in children has been limited to Xpert Ultra tongue swab testing, with low sensitivity (7-19%). Added value of this study To our knowledge, this is the first assessment of two swab-based nPOC assays for childhood TB: MiniDock MTB and MTB Ultima. In two high TB-burden settings of South Africa and Uganda, we prospectively enrolled children with presumptive TB and determined the accuracy of tongue and sputum swab testing. We found that tongue swab testing detected about half of children with culture-confirmed TB; sputum swab testing had substantially higher sensitivity than tongue swabs, and similar performance to sputum Xpert Ultra, meeting the World Health Organization (WHO) target accuracy for an nPOC sputum molecular TB test. Implications of all the available evidence The recent WHO guidelines endorsed sputum swab testing in adults and adolescents, and tongue swabs if sputum is not available. Similarly, we found that a single platform can enable nPOC molecular testing for TB among children, with sputum swab accuracy comparable to Xpert Ultra when sputum is available, and tongue swabs providing a simple, non-invasive approach to increase microbiological confirmation and potentially reduce delays in treatment when sputum is not available.

research.abstract: Abstract Cytochrome P450 (CYP) genes form a large and functionally diverse superfamily of heme-thiolate monooxygenases that catalyse the oxidation of endogenous and exogenous compounds. Within this superfamily, CYP4 enzymes primarily act on fatty acids, substrates central to energy metabolism. Sustained flight and long distance migration in birds rely on efficient fatty acid use, making CYP4 a pertinent system for examining how lipid associated functions may vary across avian lineages. Here, we characterised the evolution of CYP4 genes across 363 avian whole genomes, representing over 90% of bird families, to investigate patterns of molecular evolution and their association with ecological and life history variation. We identified four CYP4 subfamilies and analysed sequence evolution using site-models, branch-models, and branch-site models. Our analyses revealed conserved elements of the avian CYP4 repertoire alongside lineage-specific heterogeneity in selective constraint. Several amino acid sites under positive selection were located within substrate recognition sites, regions influencing substrate binding and catalysis. Branch-model analyses identified trait-associated variation in selective pressure across feeding habits, migration and primary lifestyle, with gene-specific patterns. Migration-associated differences in ω remained below one, indicating variation in the strength of selective constraint among migration categories. Branch-site analyses revealed evidence of episodic positive selection associated with migratory lineages. Overall, these results highlight site-specific adaptive evolution within CYP4 genes alongside broader variation in selective constraint, providing insight into the evolution of lipid associated metabolic pathways during avian diversification.

research.abstract: Abstract Introduction: Hepatic tuberculosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation that may mimic hepatobiliary malignancy or complex cystic lesions, resulting in diagnostic challenges. Case Presentation: A 36-year-old Filipino woman without recognized immunocompromising conditions presented with fever, weight loss, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain. Imaging showed a multiloculated cystic lesion in hepatic segments V/VI with focal biliary prominence. Liver biopsy demonstrated necrotizing and non-necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with focally positive Ziehl-Neelsen staining. Tissue MTB-PCR detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis without rifampicin resistance, and culture confirmed M. tuberculosis complex susceptible to streptomycin, isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol. CT chest showed diffuse bilateral micronodules in a miliary pattern; initial sputum smear and PCR were negative, but final sputum culture became positive at 6 weeks. Standard 2HRZE/4HR therapy was initiated, with clinical and biochemical improvement at 1 month. Conclusion: Hepatic tuberculosis should be considered in atypical cystic hepatic lesions, and tissue diagnosis is essential to avoid unnecessary invasive procedures.

research.abstract: Background Aging-related genes (ARGs) may contribute to immune heterogeneity in tuberculosis (TB), but their diagnostic and biological relevance remain incompletely defined. This study aimed to identify TB-associated ARG transcripts, characterize their immune and molecular correlates, and evaluate their exploratory diagnostic performance across prespecified cohorts. Patients and methods Public TB transcriptomic cohorts were analyzed together with a local bulk RNA-seq cohort comprising 5 TB patients and 5 controls and a local single-cell RNA-seq cohort comprising 3 active TB patients and 3 controls. The local cohorts were selected using random sampling. Age-adjusted differential expression, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, machine-learning-based feature selection, immune-infiltration analysis, consensus clustering, single-cell annotation, and Comparative Toxicogenomics Database-based compound-gene screening were performed. Results GSE83456 included 45 TB patients and 61 controls. Age-adjusted differential expression identified 189 differentially expressed genes, and the intersection of DEGs, ARGs, and blue-module genes yielded 11 discovery candidates. Nested model selection in GSE83456 identified a naive Bayes classifier based on STAT1, PLAUR, JAK2, and P2RY14. Across five repeated stratified nested cross-validation runs, the mean AUC was 0.962, with a repeat-level range of 0.954-0.969. Balanced accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were 0.926, 0.911, 0.941, and 0.928, respectively. Exploratory evaluations included GSE19439, GSE34608, GSE62525, GSE19444, and the local RNA-seq cohort. Consensus clustering separated TB samples into two ARG-associated subgroups with distinct immune-infiltration and pathway-activity profiles. CIBERSORT analysis identified significant TB-control differences in 9 of 22 inferred immune-cell types. Single-cell analysis demonstrated heterogeneous expression of STAT1, PLAUR, JAK2, and P2RY14 across annotated immune-cell subsets. CTD screening generated exploratory compound-gene associations that provide testable hypotheses for future experimental studies. Conclusion Age-adjusted multi-cohort analysis identified candidate ARG-associated TB markers and immune patterns. STAT1, PLAUR, JAK2, and P2RY14 are candidate markers rather than clinically validated biomarkers and require independent experimental and clinical validation.

research.abstract: Abstract Genome assemblies are accumulating rapidly across the Tree of Life, creating a growing need for reproducible and scalable methods for whole-genome comparison. We developed nf-core/pairgenomealign, a Nextflow workflow that automates pairwise genome alignment using the LAST software suite and produces standard alignment, visualisation, and summary outputs. The pipeline supports a wide range of evolutionary distances, runs reproducibly across local, cloud, and high-performance computing environments, and exports alignments in formats including MAF, BAM, BCF, and CRAM. We repurposed the compact format used for sequencing reads to combine the alignments of many genomes to the same target into a single file, which genome browsers display directly and from which multiple sequence alignments of any region can be extracted. Benchmarking against established genome aligners shows competitive performance with tunable trade-offs between speed and sensitivity, while applications to comparative genomics and assembly quality control illustrate its uses.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB) is able to survive and replicate within host cells of the myeloid cell lineage, a critical step in the development of active TB, achieved through multiple immune evasion mechanisms. TRPML1 (Mucolipin 1), a non-selective Ca 2+ ion channel belonging to the TRP superfamily, is predominantly expressed in innate immune cells and is localized intracellularly along the endosomal-lysosomal continuum. TRPML1-mediated Ca 2+ signalling is vital for lysosomal biogenesis and trafficking processes essential for effective immune responses. The mechanisms regulating TRPML1 channel function in myeloid cells during mycobacterial infection remain poorly characterized. METHODS: During in vitro infection, TRPML1 expression was modulated in a time-dependent manner by Mtb and M. bovis BCG in murine macrophages, as well as in human neutrophils (PMNs) and macrophages (MDMs). Using pharmacological modulation of TRPML1 channel activity, we observed alterations in intracellular Ca 2+ concentrations following Mtb infection. RESULTS: Here, we describe distinct TRPML1 expression patterns in granulomas from TB patients who had completed treatment for active TB, suggesting a potential role for TRPML1 in pathogenesis. We further demonstrate that Mtb infection is associated with altered TRPML1 expression and intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis, accompanied by changes in ROS production, necrotic cell death and enhanced mycobacterial survival within host cells. Treatment of PMN-MDM cocultures with a TRPML1 antagonist, but not an agonist, was associated with increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and necrotic cell death. DISCUSSION: Here, we show that Mtb-mediated disruption of TRPML1 function is associated with altered intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis and may contribute to impaired phagosome maturation, a process previously linked to TRPML1-dependent endolysosomal function, thereby potentially favoring mycobacterial survival within host cells. These findings suggest that Mtb-induced alterations in TRPML1 associated cellular Ca²⁺ homeostasis may impair Ca²⁺-dependent ROS production and cell death, potentially affecting intracellular Mtb survival. Our findings support a role for TRPML1 in maintaining myeloid cell Ca²⁺ homeostasis and suggest that TRPML1 may contribute to the innate immune response to Mtb infection.

research.abstract: Character recoding is a common practice in evolutionary studies. For example, phylogenies can be inferred from protein-coding DNA sequences via 61-state codon substitution models. However, often the inference is instead done by adopting 20-state amino acid replacement models that do not explicitly consider synonymous substitution. When there is substantial heterogeneity of amino acid frequencies among sites and/or among lineages, another sort of character recoding is sometimes performed. In these cases, one option is to reduce the state space of the model by placing each of the 20 amino acids into one of a relatively small number (e.g., 6) of groups of amino acids and then modeling only how group membership changes at a site over evolutionary time. Unfortunately, these kinds of character recoding schemes are prone to reducing the amount of available evolutionary information. Here, we provide a likelihood framework to statistically assess recoding schemes. Although we concentrate on the recoding of 61-state codon substitution models into 20-state amino acid replacement models, the general approach is also relevant to other recoding schemes such as those that recode 20-state models into 6-state models.

research.abstract: Abstract There is a need to breed superior wheat cultivars to meet increasing global food demand. However, modern cultivars have undergone a substantial loss of genetic diversity due to intensive breeding. A pool of genetic diversity remains untapped in wheat landraces and analysis against a single reference cannot detect genes that the reference lacks. Pangenomics can help identify genes of potential agronomic importance in these old lines that can be applied to accelerate wheat improvement. Here, we have constructed the largest wheat pangenome to date, representing 1,061 diverse individuals (827 landraces and 234 modern cultivars) from 47 countries across six continents. We identified 10,426 predicted gene models specific to landraces that are enriched for functions associated with disease resistance, abiotic stress adaptation, and symbiosis, as well as 176 landrace-specific candidate disease resistance loci. Phylogenetic analysis inferred from gene presence/absence variation reflects SNP-based ancestry-associated structure, while independent Iso-Seq data from 14 cultivars showed 96.4% concordance with cultivar-specific gene presence calls from our PAV analysis, supporting the robustness of the resource. Our results reveal that landraces harbour an extensive repertoire of genes that are absent from modern wheat cultivars and provide a foundational resource that links this gene content variation to specific accessions and ancestral groups, enabling candidate genes to be prioritised in donor lines for subsequent introgression and supporting the systematic reintroduction of adaptive variation to enhance wheat resilience and sustainability in the face of climate change.

research.abstract: Abstract Infectious diseases continue to pose a global health challenge, intensified by antimicrobial resistance and limitations of pharmaceutical countermeasures. Nanotechnology offers a promising front against these barriers using intelligent, multifunctional systems. This review explores the convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), CRISPR gene editing, bacteriophage therapy, and immune modulation within the framework of second-generation nanoparticle therapeutics. AI-guided modelling enables predictive optimization of nanoparticle design on the basis of size, charge, and surface proteins, targeting specific pathogens and providing enhanced stability. Consequently, nanoparticles serve as precision nanocarriers and protective delivery vehicles for the CRISPR-Cas system, shielding nucleic acid cargo from enzymatic degradation and enabling targeted intracellular delivery via pH-responsive endosomal escape mechanisms. The nanoparticles not only provide protection but also enable tissue-targeting and infection-site-specific delivery of the CRISPR-Cas system, facilitating precise genome editing to reverse resistance in specific pathogens such as HIV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Phage nanoparticle hybrids further expand antimicrobial potency by enhancing phage stability, delivery, and host range. Moreover, engineered nanoparticles modulate the immune system via immunosuppressive and immunostimulant strategies for reducing hyperinflammation and enhancing pathogen clearance, respectively. Despite such encouraging laboratory outcomes, the clinical translation of AI-integrated nanoparticle platforms still faces a number of obstacles. Large-scale manufacturing, scalability, and reproducibility pose a significant challenge. Regulatory approvals for such multi-modal nano-drugs seem to get bogged down due to vague and scarce exemplary proofs. Furthermore, safety and efficacy apprehensions, unpredictable and complex host-phage interactions, cost-effectiveness, and equitable access remain a subject matter of concern. Conclusively, the convergence of advanced nanotechnology, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology marks the dawn of a transformative era in infectious disease therapeutics where treatment is not only intelligent and adaptive but also ethically and globally inclusive. research.abstract: BACKGROUND: The prevalence and evolution of drug resistance in TB pose a persistent threat to global TB control. Understanding the epidemiological characteristics, population distribution, and temporal trends of drug resistance is crucial for evaluating the effectiveness of prevention and control measures and adjusting strategies accordingly. METHODS: This study retrospectively analyzed 9,665 clinical isolates of Mycobacterium TB collected between 2015 and 2024. Drug susceptibility testing was performed using the proportion method to detect resistance to isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, streptomycin, and levofloxacin. The chi-square test was used to compare differences between groups, and the chi-square test for trend was applied to analyze temporal changes in drug resistance. RESULTS: The overall drug resistance rate was 20.87% (2017/9665, 95% CI: 20.06%-21.69%), and the MDR rate was 10.25% (991/9665, 95% CI: 9.66%-10.88%). Drug resistance rates varied significantly among different populations, with males (1528/6730,22.70%; 95% CI: 21.71%-23.72%) exhibiting higher rates than females (489/2935,16.66%; 95% CI: 15.33%-18.06%), and the 19-59 age group (1511/6788,22.26%; 95% CI: 21.27%-23.27%) showing higher rates than the ≤ 18 (124/694,17.87%; 95% CI: 15.09%-20.92%) and ≥ 60 age groups (382/2183, 17.50%; 95% CI: 15.93%-19.16%). Over the ten-year period, the overall drug resistance rate showed a significant upward trend (from 17.29% to 22.98%). Rates of single drug resistance, PDR, and resistance to streptomycin and levofloxacin also increased significantly. In contrast, the MDR rate and resistance rates to rifampicin and ethambutol did not show significant trends. CONCLUSION: The TB drug resistance problem in this region is severe, with a rapid increase in resistance to the key second-line drug levofloxacin, indicating significant challenges for the current prevention and control system. Targeted interventions for populations with higher resistance rates, such as males and young adults, along with strengthened antibiotic stewardship, are critical to curbing the further spread of drug resistance.

research.abstract: Abstract Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) complicates bacterial infection management, motivating genomic approaches to predicting antibiotic susceptibility. This study assessed the predictive performance and generalisability of machine-learning models using resistance-associated genomic features from Escherichia coli. Publicly available genomic and phenotypic records yielded 446 genomes, 252 binary genomic features and 1,935 susceptibility observations across nine antibiotics. Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers were compared using validation ROC-AUC, followed by evaluation on held-out test subsets. Additional analyses examined identical genomic feature profiles across partitions, performance across source publications and feature redundancy. Ampicillin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole achieved held-out accuracies of 93.98% and 93.59%, ROC-AUC values of 0.912 and 0.954, and resistant-isolate recall of 95.16% and 94.55%, respectively. In contrast, ceftazidime achieved 88.52% accuracy and 0.940 ROC-AUC but identified only 22.22% of resistant isolates. Seventy-four held-out observations shared identical 252-feature profiles with training isolates; all were correctly classified. After excluding overlapping observations without retraining, ROC-AUC decreased from 0.912 to 0.848 for ampicillin and from 0.954 to 0.901 for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Exploratory cross-publication evaluations showed variable performance, with shared multilocus sequence types in 16 of 18 comparisons. Reducing genomic features did not materially alter validation performance in the two antibiotics examined. These findings indicate that genomic predictors can discriminate resistance phenotypes, but aggregate accuracy may obscure poor resistant-isolate detection. The findings also distinguish performance on conventionally held-out isolates from performance on previously unseen resistance-feature profiles, an important consideration when bacterial population structure and correlated determinants substantially influence model evaluation. Independent phylogenetic and prospective validation remains necessary before clinical use.

research.abstract: Abstract Canine distemper virus (CDV) has recently been detected in New Zealand fur seals ( Arctocephalus forsteri ), including retrospective samples from 2020 and outbreaks associated with substantial mortality in late 2024 and 2025. However, the geographic distribution of CDV and the broader viral diversity harboured by New Zealand fur seals remain poorly understood. Characterising the fur seal virome can provide insights into viral diversity, dispersal and the occurrence of viral co-infections, while assessing the distribution of CDV across colonies. We used metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise the viromes of 178 live and recently deceased fur seals sampled from four large fur seal colonies (Kaikōura, Dunedin, West Coast and Wairarapa). We investigated viral diversity, community composition and geographic structure using phylogenetic analyses to examine viral evolutionary relationships and CDV distribution. We identified 23 viral species, including 20 putatively novel species. Several were related to viruses previously identified in terrestrial mammals. One viral species was detected across geographically separated colonies, while several other closely related viruses were identified across colonies, with viral sharing most frequent between Kaikōura and Wairarapa. Viral diversity was similar between live and recently deceased fur seals, while community composition showed geographic structuring. CDV was detected only in Kaikōura, where the lineage associated with the 2024 outbreak remained in circulation. No CDV was detected in the other sampled colonies. This study reveals substantial previously undocumented viral diversity in New Zealand fur seals, improving our understanding of viral distribution and CDV circulation in marine mammal populations.

research.abstract: Abstract Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci associated with Type 2 Diabetes (T2D), yet pinpointing specific causal genes and their relevant cellular contexts remains a critical bottleneck. To address this gap, we developed CELL-X, a novel computational framework systematically integrating fine-mapped genetic evidence with high-resolution single-cell transcriptomics and disease progression dynamics. Utilizing a custom out-of-memory processing engine, we analyzed an integrated human pancreatic islet atlas of 245,878 cells without forced data downsampling. We evaluated 37 genetically supported T2D candidate genes, quantifying cell-type relevance via a max-scaled Cell Relevance Score (CRS). Disease-associated transcriptional dynamics were subsequently incorporated using a Disease Relevance Score (DRS) based on heterogeneous expression shifts across normal, prediabetic, and T2D metabolic states. CELL-X successfully identified beta cells as the dominant disease-relevant cellular context and prioritized established causal genes, including SLC30A8, GLIS3, GCK, and TCF7L2. Validation against a 30-gene benchmark demonstrated exceptional target recovery and significant metabolic pathway enrichment. Furthermore, rigorous statistical null modeling confirmed this prioritization is driven by true biological variance rather than background transcriptomic noise. Ultimately, CELL-X provides a highly scalable, robust framework for generating biologically informed hypotheses in complex polygenic disease research.

research.abstract: Abstract Alongside the proposal of the taxon Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni for 16SrIII (X-Disease) group, the designation “ Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni-related strains” was proposed for strains that were closely related to the taxon based on multilocus sequence characterization. However, recent genome-based studies have created taxonomic ambiguity by either assigning related strains directly to the taxon Ca. P. pruni or separating them into more than one genomic cluster without formal taxonomic classification or proposing new taxon for new divergent strains. In this study, we sequenced genomes of the pecan bunchy top phytoplasma (PBT), previously designated a “ Ca. P. pruni-related strain,” initially to confirm the pathogen in an Oklahoma pecan orchard. Phylogenomic comparisons with previously sequenced Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni strains revealed four well-supported taxonomic groups based on average nucleotide identity, digital DNA–DNA hybridization, and phylogenetic analyses, with different host ecologies consistent with International Research Programme on Comparative Mycoplasmology (IRPCM) guidelines for assigning new taxon. Accordingly, we propose a reclassification of Ca. P. pruni and related strains into four species: Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni, representing the taxon associated with X-disease phytoplasma; three proposed new Candidatus species including Candidatus Phytoplasma caryae sp. nov, Candidatus Phytoplasma conii sp. nov and Candidatus Phytoplasma lactucae sp. nov. The study provides comparative-genomic insights into these taxonomic groups that support their evolution.

research.abstract: Childhood adversity (CA) is one of the strongest risk factors for psychiatric but also numerous medical disorders, yet only a subset of exposed individuals develops these outcomes. Gene-by-environment interactions have long been proposed to account for this variability, but identifying the specific variants involved has proven difficult in studies using clinical endpoints. We therefore mapped interaction effects between genetic variants and CA at the molecular level, testing for contextual methylation quantitative trait loci (contmeQTLs) in peripheral blood from 3,471 adolescents and adults across six cohorts. Meta-analysis identified 5,120 contmeQTLs, >99% acting in cis, of which 20% were already detectable in three independent childhood cohorts (N=780), indicating that these effects emerge in temporal proximity to exposure. ContmeQTLs were enriched for immune-related pathways, particularly the major histocompatibility (MHC)/human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-complex, were associated with altered expression of HLA and other immune regulators, and captured disease risk beyond that explained by baseline meQTLs. A polygenic interaction responsivity score, constructed from contmeQTL variants, predicted both a larger acute transcriptional response to infection and a greater shift towards a pro-inflammatory plasma profile in CA-exposed adults, including in UK Biobank. Using ancient DNA, we found that these responsive alleles have been under positive selection, identifying molecular responsivity to adversity as an evolutionarily shaped trait whose benefit under acute challenge is accompanied by liability to immune-mediated and psychiatric disease.

research.abstract: Abstract Micromonas polaris is the dominant picoeukaryote of the Arctic Ocean, where it sustains primary production across habitats from sea ice to open water to the subsurface chlorophyll maximum. How a single species maintains this ecological breadth has remained unclear. Standard phylogenetic markers such as 18S rRNA are nearly invariant within M. polaris and conceal any internal genomic heterogeneity the species may possess. Here we present a pangenome of 14 M. polaris strains spanning the Arctic basin, integrated with Tara Oceans metagenomes, that resolves the species into two diverged ecotypes invisible to 18S rRNA but recovered consistently by prp8 , genome-wide SNPs, ANI, and orthogroup-based phylogenies. The two ecotypes coexist sympatrically, with one lineage consistently enriched deeper in the water column across the basin. M. polaris carries 990 polar-specific hierarchical orthogroups absent from temperate Micromonas , organised around one-carbon metabolism, endocytosis, transmembrane transport, and photo-oxidative stress response. Several components show phylogenetic signatures of horizontal acquisition from co-occurring marine taxa. Atlantification is bringing temperate Micromonas into Arctic margins seasonally, but the polar night likely limits their year-round persistence. M. polaris and its polar-specific toolkit appear positioned to persist through the dark season, suggesting Arctic margins will undergo seasonal turnover rather than stable replacement.

research.abstract: Abstract Introgression introduced deeply diverged archaic variation into modern human populations and contributed to local adaptation. In Indigenous American populations, however, the landscape of adaptive introgression remains poorly resolved. Genome-wide scans have reported numerous candidate loci, but complex demographic histories and recent admixture make genuine signals difficult to distinguish from false positives. Here, we systematically re-evaluated previously reported candidates of adaptive introgression in Peruvians using a multilayered framework and refined more than 150 putative signals to 25 high-confidence candidate loci with concordant evidence of Neanderthal- or Denisovan-like ancestry and positive selection. Using ancestral recombination graph (ARG) approaches, we inferred selection onset windows for 21 loci. These onsets were non-uniformly distributed across Peruvian population history, revealing temporally dynamic selection without robust evidence for a fixed number of discrete waves. Together with pre-Columbian ancient DNA evidence, the inferred histories support the inheritance of the candidate adaptive archaic haplotypes through ancestral Native American populations rather than first introduction through post-Columbian admixture. Functional analyses identified network-level signals consistent with polygenic selection in lipid metabolic and immune-related pathways, elevated regulatory effects predicted across archaic haplotypes, and occasional coding variation of potential functional relevance, including a missense variant at the immune-related gene CXCR4 . Our results show that archaic introgressed variation remained evolutionarily important and available to selection long after introgression, providing a reservoir of genetic variation that could be repeatedly recruited by selection at different points in American population history. Significance Statement Archaic variants reached the Americas through populations already carrying Neanderthal and Denisovan ancestry, offering an opportunity to study adaptation far from the original contact zone. Scans of American populations have reported more putative adaptive introgression loci than realistically expected, partly because the complex demographic histories make true signals difficult to distinguish from false positives. Reconstructing selection histories at credible loci may in turn help constrain that history. Here we identify 25 high-confidence candidate regions in Peruvians, among which 21 have inferred selection onsets predating European contact, and archaic-associated alleles from all 25 are present in pre-Columbian American ancient genomes. Functional analyses find pathway-level selection signals, predicted regulatory effects, and occasional evolutionarily interesting missense variants, including at the immune-related gene CXCR4 .

research.abstract: Introduction TB incidence in Suriname has remained stable over the last decade. Understanding transmission patterns is essential for developing effective TB control strategies to interrupt ongoing transmission. Methods We conducted a descriptive analysis of routinely collected demographic and clinical data combined with whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data. Patients were classified into large (>6 patients) clusters, small (2-6 patients) clusters, or as non-clustered cases (unique). Bivariate and multivariable analyses compared patients in large clusters with those in small clusters and non-clustered patients. Epidemiological links obtained through patient interviews were compared with WGS findings. Results Of 698 TB patients notified during 2019-2024, WGS data were available for 368 (53%); 85% belonged to a genomic cluster. Indigenous ethnicity was inversely associated with membership in a large versus a small cluster (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 0.3; 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.1-0.6). Compared with non-clustered cases, patients in large clusters were more likely to report illicit drug use (aOR = 3.0; 95% CI = 1.1-8.9). Conclusion WGS provided detailed insights into Mycobacterium tuberculosis transmission in Suriname. Illicit drug use was associated with membership in large transmission clusters, highlighting the need for early case finding and strengthened collaboration between TB and substance-use services.

research.abstract: Public genome collections underpin our understanding of bacterial diversity and the distribution of traits such as antibiotic resistance, and increasingly serve as training data for genomic foundation models. Their growing size promises an increasingly complete view of microbial genetic variation. However, these collections combine studies with different sampling priorities, often overrepresenting subgroups of closely related strains of particular interest. The resulting bias reduces effective information, and its consequences for diversity estimates and the value of further sequencing remain insufficiently quantified. Here we show that accounting for this escalating sampling bias is essential for accurate gene frequency estimates and hints at greater genomic diversity than current data suggest. We propose to detect and reduce sampling bias based on phylogenetic relationships compared to expectations under random sampling, which, in contrast to dereplication and data reduction methods, preserves fine-scale diversity in large samples. Applied to 402 prokaryotic species in the NCBI genome database, our method PhyloThin indicates that the effective number of samples is 41% lower than the actual number but retains more than twice as many genomes as dereplication. Sampling bias varies substantially among species, showing that genome counts alone provide an incomplete measure of how well a species has already been characterized. PhyloThin thus turns biased, expanding genome collections into more representative samples for studying genome evolution and population genetic inference with implications for training genomic foundation models, pathogen surveillance, and the discovery of novel genetic functions.
