research.abstract: Importance: Large-scale plasma proteomic studies have linked hundreds of proteins to psychiatric disorders, but it is unclear which reflect causal biology rather than confounding or consequences of illness. Objective: To determine which plasma proteins associated with depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, and psychotic disorders have genetic evidence of a causal role. Design, Setting, and Participants: This proteogenomic study combined genetic analyses with cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses in the UK Biobank (UKB) cohort (N=52,615). Associations of 2,923 plasma proteins were tested using two-sample Mendelian randomisation (MR) and genetic colocalisation with common-variant protein quantitative trait loci (pQTLs) from the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project (N=34,557). Findings were appraised via a rule-based framework combining instrument validity with genetic analyses using blood and brain expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) and rare-variant MR. Exposures: Measured and genetically proxied plasma protein levels. Main Outcomes and Measures: Prevalent and incident diagnoses of depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, and psychotic disorders; summary statistics from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia. Results: A total of 1,685 proteins were involved in protein-disorder associations in UKB after multiple testing correction, of which 26 proteins (32 protein-disorder pairs) met both MR and colocalisation (MR false discovery rate <0.05 and posterior probability of colocalisation [≥]0.8). After independent genetic validation, 9 disorder-protein pairs involving 7 proteins (CD40, ADAM22, CDHR1, PDIA3, SEMA3F, DSG3, and DDR1) met criteria for credible causal evidence, led by CD40, an immune signalling receptor, for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Specifically, higher genetically predicted CD40 levels were associated with lower risk of schizophrenia (odds ratio [OR] 0.90; 95%CI 0.85-0.95) and bipolar disorder (OR 0.89; 95%CI 0.84-0.95), supported by directionally concordant colocalised brain eQTL and rare-variant MR evidence. Conclusions and Relevance: Few plasma protein associations with major psychiatric disorders had credible genetic support for causality, demonstrating that multi-layer appraisal across molecular layers, tissues, and genetic variant classes is required before nominating proteomic targets. CD40, an immune receptor targeted by drugs in clinical development, showed robust protective genetic support across schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, warranting focused mechanistic and therapeutic investigation.

research.abstract: Abstract Pollen tube reception (PTR) is essential for fertilization and can act as a prezygotic barrier in interspecific crosses. While core female components such as LORELEI (LRE) and FERONIA (FER) mediate conspecific PTR, their roles in heterospecific compatibility remain unclear. Here, we investigated how LRE sequence variation influences PTR outcomes with heterospecific pollen in Brassicaceae. In Arabidopsis thaliana , PTR frequently failed when ovules were pollinated with Arabidopsis lyrata or Sisymbrium irio , and loss of LRE or FER further increased pollen tube overgrowth in a pollen-species-dependent manner. Complementation of lre ovules with LRE orthologs showed distinct, donor-dependent effects: AlyLRE and SiLRE produced modest and variable improvements with A. lyrata pollen, whereas SiLRE consistently and markedly improved reception of S. irio pollen. Evolutionary analyses indicated relaxed purifying selection in the LRE lineage relative to its paralog LLG1 and nominated residues 47 and 120 as candidates for functional divergence. Consistent with this, the Lineage II-associated R120T substitution enhanced reception of S. irio pollen while partially reducing conspecific PTR. In addition, the ancestral-state E47P–R120G combination also improved heterospecific PTR without measurably compromising conspecific function. Together, these results indicate that LRE sequence diversification can modulate female-side compatibility with pollen tubes from different evolutionary lineages, potentially by altering how pollen tube-derived signals are sensed and transduced during reception.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Type 2 Diabetes mellites and Metabolic syndrome are global public health problems, and their burden is rising, particularly in developing countries. Metabolic syndrome (syndrome X, insulin resistance syndrome) consists of a constellation of metabolic abnormalities that confer increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and diabetes mellitus. There are limited data on prevalence of metabolic syndrome in type II DM patients in Ethiopia and in the horn of Africa at large, and no research has been done in our institution on this topic. Objective To determine the prevalence of metabolic syndrome and its associated factors in patients with type 2 diabetes on follow up at Asella Referral and Teaching Hospital diabetes follow up clinic, Asella, Oromia, Ethiopia. Method Cross-sectional, prospective, hospital-based survey was conducted to assess the prevalence of metabolic syndrome and its associated factors in type II DM patients among those who visited diabetic follow-up clinic of Asella referral and teaching Hospital. All type II DM patients, who visited the diabetic follow-up clinic in the study period was included in the study. 285 participants were selected using systemic random sampling technique. Data was collected from patients and their chart and filled on a checklist by trained data collectors. Data was entered to epi-data cleared and analyzed by SPSS version 26.0 and Odds ratio with 95% CI and P-value of <0.05 was considered for declaring level of significance. Results Using the NCEP-ATP III criteria the magnitude of Metabolic syndrome was 75.1% in this study. Among the components of Metabolic syndrome high blood pressure was the commonest (70.9%) followed by low HDL Cholesterol (70.5%), high Triglyceride (46%) and high Waist circumference (12.6%) respectively. Female and Male had comparable prevalence of Metabolic syndrome and the study showed that 55.4% of participants were taking Lipid lowering medications. Multivariate logistic regression analysis showed four factors; frequency of taking Meat (AOR = 2.47; 95% CI = 1.323-4.6), Alcohol intake (AOR = 2.79; 95% CI = 1.146-6.806), total Cholesterol level (AOR = 2.72; 95% CI = 1.023-7.224) and LDL Cholesterol level (AOR = 2.31; 95% CI = (1.029-5.161) were significantly associated with Metabolic syndrome according to this study. Conclusion In this study the magnitude of Metabolic syndrome was found to be 75.1% and the associated factors were Alcohol intake, Frequency of taking Meat, Total and LDL Cholesterol level. Recommendation Counseling of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus patients on the need of decreasing Alcohol and Meat consumption and physicians need to improve the habit of prescribing Lipid lowering medication.

research.abstract: Pathogen genomic surveillance works from raw reads, assembled genomes and alignments, representations that are slow and costly to compare at scale. Compact embeddings from genomic language models offer an alternative, but surveillance requires resolving both evolutionary ancestry (phylogeny) and phenotypic capability (function) - which need not co-vary. Here we present MicroDUET, which adapts a 26.6-million-parameter ProkBERT backbone with two 3.5-million-parameter adapter heads: a phylogeny head trained contrastively on genome windows from the same microbes, and a function head trained to identify genes across taxa. On held-out retrieval benchmarks, the phylogeny head returned the correct species for 80.3% and 66.6% of cellular and viral queries, and the function head the correct gene family for 97.3% and 97.2%, reaching 74.4% accuracy on an independent antimicrobial resistance-class benchmark. Across all three benchmarks MicroDUET outranked 17 other genomic encoders. MicroDUET therefore provides a compact, reusable representation for scalable pathogen surveillance and sequence triage.

research.abstract: Empyema necessitans is a rare complication of pleural infection in which infected pleural fluid extends through the parietal pleura into the surrounding soft tissues. We report the case of a 32-year-old man of Indian origin living in the United Kingdom who presented with worsening right-sided pleuritic chest pain, several months of night sweats, and a persistent dry cough. Five months earlier, he had been treated for right-sided pneumonia complicated by a pleural effusion, with persistent radiographic abnormalities on follow-up. Examination revealed reduced right-sided air entry and a tender, fluctuant swelling over the right posterior chest wall. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated a posterior pleural collection extending through the chest wall into the adjacent paraspinal musculature, consistent with empyema necessitans. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded frank purulent fluid. Routine bacterial, anaerobic, and fungal cultures were negative. Acid-fast bacilli were not seen on initial microscopy; however, mycobacterial culture became positive after seven days, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of the pleural fluid detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. Whole-genome sequencing subsequently identified a lineage 1 East-African-Indian-Ocean isolate with predicted susceptibility to first-line antituberculous agents. Four-drug antituberculous therapy was commenced, with subsequent clinical and radiological improvement. This case highlights chest wall swelling as an unusual presentation of tuberculosis and emphasizes the importance of cross-sectional imaging and targeted mycobacterial testing in establishing the diagnosis.

research.abstract: Abstract Objectives Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa airway infections can persist for years despite intensive antibiotic therapy guided by standard antimicrobial susceptibility testing. While this technique captures the emergence of resistance, it does not reproduce many features of the infection environment, where adaptation acquired during chronic infection may alter bacterial responses to antibiotics in ways that are not fully reflected by conventional susceptibility testing. Here we investigated antibiotic responses of longitudinal clinical isolates under standard laboratory conditions and in an airway epithelial infection model. Methods Six longitudinal pairs of P. aeruginosa isolates from people with cystic fibrosis were analysed. Changes in bacterial growth following exposure to tobramycin, ceftazidime and ciprofloxacin were quantified under standard laboratory conditions and compared with changes in bacterial burden after treatment measured in differentiated airway epithelial cultures maintained under air-liquid interface (ALI) conditions that reproduce key features of the airway infection environment. Representative phenotypes were visualized by confocal microscopy and interpreted in the context of available whole-genome sequencing data. Results Major resistance phenotypes identified by conventional susceptibility testing were largely reproduced in the ALI model. However, concordance between phenotypes observed under standard laboratory and ALI conditions differed between antibiotics. Several isolates classified as susceptible according to conventional susceptibility testing displayed substantial survival in the ALI model, and these discordant phenotypes were observed predominantly among those isolates recovered after prolonged airway persistence. Genomic analyses identified mutations associated with both classical resistance mechanisms and chronic adaptation. Conclusions Phenotypes observed under conventional laboratory conditions do not uniformly predict those observed in the ALI airway conditions. Discordant phenotypes were most apparent among chronically adapted isolates and varied between antibiotics, suggesting that adaptation acquired during chronic infection can alter antibiotic responses in ways that are not fully reflected by conventional susceptibility testing.

research.abstract: Abstract Local adaptation is contingent on genotype-by-environment interactions, which are often mediated by variation in gene expression. The causes and consequences of variation in gene expression are complex, and they are rarely evaluated under the multi-dimensional environmental regimes that occur in the field. Here, we investigate switchgrass gene expression variation in contrasting sites in Michigan and Texas. We examined differentially expressed genes between upland and lowland switchgrass genotypes and found that genes with genotype x environment (GxE) interactions were enriched for GO terms related to phosphorus metabolism. After mapping expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) in a switchgrass diversity panel in both sites, we compared distinct categories of eQTL to investigate their effects on gene expression in contrasting environments and their evolutionary history. Cis regulatory variants are more likely to have consistent effects across sites, while trans regulatory variants were more likely to have site-specific effects, and are more likely to underlie changes in gene expression between sites. Lower minor allele frequency in trans regulatory variants is consistent with stronger purifying selection. Furthermore, site-specific regulatory variants exhibited intermediate minor allele frequencies, consistent with balancing selection or soft sweeps. Finally, motivated by enrichment for phosphorus-related genes exhibiting differential expression between sites, we conducted a GWAS for leaf phosphorus concentration in the diversity panel. By overlaying the GWAS results with the eQTL map, we characterized cis and trans regulation of candidate genes for leaf P concentration in Michigan and Texas. Together, this work provides novel insights on the molecular basis and evolutionary history of GxE interactions in switchgrass.

research.abstract: Bacterial species can be separated by billions of years of evolution. However, studies of such ancient relationships often rely on methods developed for eukaryotes, which are less diverse. Such methods can regard instances of horizontal gene transfer as contamination, rely heavily on a species phylogeny when partitioning paralogs, and fail to account for the multi-domain architectures of some genes. Here, we introduce, showcase, and benchmark bofasa, a software for high-quality and automated inference of ortholog groups across distantly related bacterial species. bofasa employs a recursive algorithm to split coarse homolog groups into paralogous subsets and first establishes domain-level ortholog groups prior to assessing evolutionary relationships between entire proteins. In comparison to other methods commonly used for multi-species bacterial comparative genomics, bofasa is substantially more conservative in predicting orthology yet can often recover the largest single-copy core genome. Beyond orthology inference, the software also features several additional utility functionalities, including assessment of which ortholog groups are commonly found on mobile genetic elements or possess variable genomic contexts.

research.abstract: Multidrug efflux pumps are major drivers of antimicrobial resistance, but overlapping resistance mechanisms mask the physiological limits of efflux alone. Bacterial genomes encode a large repertoire of multidrug efflux pumps, which could theoretically combine to achieve exceptionally high levels of resistance. To delineate the extent of resistance achievable through efflux driven adaptation, we performed adaptive laboratory evolution of Mycobacterium smegmatis mc²155 wild-type and efflux-deleted (ΔlfrA, ΔefpA) strains against ethidium bromide, a broad-spectrum efflux substrate. Despite prolonged selection, resistance reproducibly plateaued at 8-16 fold increase in MIC under the tested conditions. This plateau emerged through distinct evolutionary trajectories characterized by non-overlapping efflux pump sets: from overexpression of the well-characterized lfrA to upregulation of multiple uncharacterized pumps, all conferring cross-resistance. Genetic reconstruction of mutations in a transcriptional regulator and a membrane protein, together with overexpression of efflux pumps, recapitulated the resistance phenotypes of the evolved strains. Sustained pump overexpression depleted membrane potential and drove metabolic suppression, suggesting that energetic exhaustion may constrain further increase in efflux-mediated resistance. Similar constraints were observed in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, indicating that they may extend to other mycobacterial species. Efflux-metabolic integration thus affects resistance evolution, revealing therapeutic vulnerabilities to combat multidrug resistance.

research.abstract: The Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) is a genetically conserved group of pathogens whose lineage diversity has important biological, clinical, epidemiological, and public health implications. Human- and animal-adapted MTBC lineages differ in phylogeographic distribution, host association, transmission, drug resistance patterns, phenotypic traits, and diagnostic relevance. This narrative review summarizes the currently described MTBC lineages, including geographically restricted and recently recognized groups, and examines how lineage and sublineage structure can influence these characteristics. It also examines classical and genomic genotyping approaches, including IS 6110 -restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP), spoligotyping, mycobacterial interspersed repetitive unit-variable number tandem repeat (MIRU-VNTR), and SNP-based classification using whole-genome sequencing (WGS), with particular emphasis on lineage-dependent differences in discriminatory performance and phylogenetic resolution. Particular attention is given to lineage-associated variation in transmission, drug resistance, cell envelope composition, diagnostic interpretation, and genomic surveillance. This review also addresses inconsistencies between historical and genomic nomenclature. Integrating harmonized classification, broader genomic sampling, clinical, epidemiological, and phenotypic data will improve interpretation of MTBC diversity and its application to tuberculosis surveillance and control.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) in Oman remains above the pre-elimination threshold of the End TB Strategy, largely due to cases among the expatriate population. Pyrazinamide (PZA), a key first-line anti-TB drug that shortens treatment duration, is increasingly threatened by rising PZA resistance (PZA-R). This study analyzed 241 Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) isolates collected across Oman between 2018 and 2023, including PZA-resistant (PZA-R) (n = 105) and PZA-susceptible (PZA-S) (n = 74) isolates. Drug susceptibility testing was performed using BD MGIT SIRE/PZA kits. Mutations in candidate PZA resistance genes (pncA, panD, and rpsA) and spoligotype profiles were assessed, while a subset of 96 isolates underwent whole-genome sequencing (WGS). MTB isolates showed high genetic diversity, comprising ten clades across four major lineages, with PZA-R predominating in lineage 1. Mutations in pncA, panD, and rpsA showed low sensitivity (≈10%) but high specificity (97.5%) for detecting PZA-R. Consistent with these findings, WGS showed poor concordance with phenotypic PZA resistance (κ = 0.15), but accurately predicted resistance to rifampicin (κ = 0.85) and isoniazid (κ = 0.79). Genome-wide association analysis identified 16 genes associated with PZA-R; however, the detected variants were not consistently linked to the resistant phenotype, suggesting lineage-specific polymorphisms or compensatory adaptations. Phylogenetic analysis revealed substantial diversity, with PZA-R isolates distributed across multiple lineages differing by more than 50 SNPs. These findings highlight substantial genotype-phenotype discordance in PZA resistance and support further studies integrating quantitative phenotyping and genomic analysis. Further genomic studies can therefore improve resistance prediction and monitoring of the spread of drug resistance.

research.abstract: Bacterial genomes encode a diverse array of proteins that function in a coordinated manner to orchestrate the highly dynamic process of cell division. Over the course of evolution, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mt) and related mycobacterial species have diverged from the model bacterial species such as E. coli and B. subtilis and acquired distinct, poorly conserved proteins that underpin their distinct mechanisms of growth and division. However, the identity and functional roles of these molecular determinants remain largely elusive. In the present study, we identified two additional Di Viva domain-containing proteins of mycobacteria, Msm0050 and Msm5083, and performed detailed functional characterization of Msm5083/Rv1209, thereby expanding the known repertoire of DivIVA domain-containing proteins in this species. Although homologous to Wag31 and SepIVA (the known mycobacterial DivIVA domain-containing proteins), they show distinct cell division defects. Functional studies using an Msm5083 deletion mutant highlighted its role in lipid biosynthesis and maintaining cell envelope integrity, and hence, we named it CidIVA (cell envelope integrity determinant DivIVA). Subcellular localization and interactome analysis demonstrated that it homes to the membrane and interacts with other membrane-associated proteins involved in membrane synthesis and maintenance, lipid metabolism, and transportation, consistent with the observed phenotypes. Interestingly, Rv1209, the orthologue of Msm5083, showed enrichment at the poles and lateral cell wall and predominant interactions with virulence-related proteins. Although dispensable for in vitro survival , it is required for Mtb survival in vivo . Overall, our study identifies two novel DivIVA domain-containing proteins, one of which forms a functional nexus linking lipid homeostasis, cell-envelope maintenance and cell division. These results not only advance our understanding of mycobacterial cell biology but also suggest broader principles of functional diversification within multi-member protein families across bacterial species.

research.abstract: Abstract Relationships among the five subfamilies of Linnina within Dipsacales remain contentious. Extensive nuclear gene-tree discordance and cytonuclear discordance involving Linnaeoideae complicate reconstruction of their early evolutionary history. We analyzed whole-genome resequencing data from 88 Dipsacales species representing all nine subfamilies and eight outgroups. Using Dipsacales-specific nuclear reference locus sets, we recovered 3,023 orthologous nuclear loci. Nuclear analyses consistently placed (Morinoideae + Zabelioideae) sister to (Linnaeoideae + (Valerianoideae + Dipsacoideae)) across inference methods and character-coding schemes. Despite strong backbone support, extensive gene-tree discordance persisted at deep nodes. Node-level analyses suggested that incomplete lineage sorting (ILS) was a major source of discordance, while evidence for ancient gene flow varied among nodes. At the Linnaeoideae + (Valerianoideae + Dipsacoideae) node, topology frequencies approached ILS-only expectations, whereas internal branch lengths supported a model incorporating gene flow. At the Morinoideae + Zabelioideae node, multiple analyses provided more consistent evidence of ancient gene flow. ILS-only simulations recovered the observed plastid placement of Linnaeoideae in 8.63% of replicates, indicating that ILS could generate this topology; ancient gene flow, potentially involving plastid capture, remains a possible explanation for the cytonuclear discordance. Divergence-time estimates placed four major Linnina backbone divergences between 56.87 and 48.77 Ma. These findings suggest that early Linnina diversification involved successive lineage divergences and extensive ancestral polymorphism sorting, potentially accompanied by ancient gene exchange among some ancestral lineages. research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background The concurrent infection of Tuberculosis (TB) and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) constitutes a significant clinical challenge and public health emergency throughout Sub-Saharan Africa. Although national healthcare systems provide complimentary diagnostic and treatment services, early-stage mortality rates among individuals with dual infections remain critically elevated. This investigation seeks to determine independent clinical, immunological, behavioral, and geographic factors associated with mortality outcomes in TB/HIV co-infected populations within the Bénoué Department of North Cameroon, employing district-level primary analytical modeling supplemented by secondary sensitivity analyses to mitigate potential bias from limited data availability. Methods A mixed retrospective and prospective cohort investigation was described, encompassing 406 co-infected individuals receiving treatment across all 14 Diagnostic and Treatment Centers (CDTs) distributed throughout the 8 health districts of the department during the period from January 1, 2022, through December 31, 2023, with extension of tuberculosis monitoring treatment ended on November 30, 2024. Statistical analysis conducted using SPSS version 25 incorporated preliminary bivariate Chi-square testing (p < 0.05) succeeded by primary multivariate binary logistic regression modeling and a supplementary sensitivity analysis stratifying geographic location into urban central versus combined peripheral and rural district categories [1-26]. Results Among 3,883 patients initiating tuberculosis treatment, 406 had concurrent HIV infection (10.46% prevalence). This co-infected group experienced significantly higher mortality at 15.02% (61/406), accounting for 84.72% (61/72) of all tuberculosis-related deaths in the department (p < 0.05). Multivariate analysis identified multiple independent mortality risk factors: geographic location in outlying districts (Gashiga: AOR = 56.81 [1.52–2127.84], p = 0.029; Garoua II: AOR = 48.36 [3.10–755.42], p = 0.006; Pitoa: AOR = 48.21 [2.53– 918.98], p = 0.010; Lagdo: AOR = 28.63 [1.70–481.03], p = 0.020), severe immunosuppression at WHO Stage III (AOR = 9.88 [2.28–42.89], p = 0.002) and Stage IV (AOR = 10.81 [4.77– 24.54], p < 0.001), inadequate medication adherence (AOR = 4.86 [1.14–20.69], p = 0.033), and elevated viral load (AOR = 7.46 [1.73–32.25], p = 0.007). A secondary sensitivity analysis that combined outlying district categories substantially decreased standard errors from 1.849 to 0.485 and generated a precise 95% confidence interval (AOR = 9.40 [3.63–24.32], p < 0.001), confirming that unequal healthcare access in rural areas represents a critical driver of excess mortality. Conclusion The heightened early mortality in TB/HIV co-infected individuals in North Cameroon stems from geographic variations in healthcare availability, late clinical diagnosis, poor medication compliance, and gaps in viral load monitoring systems. Reducing this mortality requires introducing rapid point-of-care viral load testing, establishing accessible molecular diagnostic facilities across regions, and deploying community-based programs to improve treatment compliance.

research.abstract: Computing phylogenetic likelihoods becomes challenging when the continuous-time Markov chain has a large state space. At each branch, pruning algorithms require terms of the form $e^{Q t}\cdot B$, where $Q$ is an $S \times S$ rate matrix (e.g., for $S$ states), $t$ is a branch length, and the columns of matrix $B$ (e.g., $B \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{S \times L}$) are partial-likelihood vectors for $L$ site patterns. Many implementations calculate the dense transition matrix $P(t)=e^{Q t}$ via eigendecomposition and multiply it by $B$. This strategy is efficient for small state spaces, but it can be inefficient for large sparse rate matrices because forming $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices destroys sparsity and its cost may not be well amortized when $L$ is small. We implement an alternative likelihood kernel based on the Al-Mohy and Higham (2011) algorithm for computing the action of the matrix exponential directly, avoiding explicit construction of $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices. The resulting method takes full advantage of the sparsity of $Q$. We implement this method as a CPU-based extension to the BEAGLE library and evaluate it on two large-state molecular models: a Markov-modulated codon model of heterotachy with $M$ selective regimes and $61\cdot M$ possible states, and a codon-pair model of interlocus gene conversion between two paralogs with $61^2=3\,721$ possible states. Our results characterize when action-based likelihood computation improves performance over calculating $e^{Q t}$ directly. We show that this method enables fast, scalable inference for complex models, removing a key computational barrier to the study of evolution with large state space models.

research.abstract: Abstract Horizontal gene transfer mediated by conjugative plasmids is a primary driver of bacterial evolution and the spread of adaptive traits, including antibiotic resistance determinants. Tracking how these plasmids disseminate through complex microbial communities remains a major challenge. Current methodologies often yield static, endpoint snapshots of host identity, overlooking transient transfer events and plasmid encounters with the co-resident mobilome. To overcome these limitations, we introduce SPacer Integration (SPI) plasmids, which turn the mobile element itself into a recorder of its own transfer history. We engineered conjugative and mobilizable plasmids to carry a CRISPR-Cas adaptation cassette ( cas1–cas2 and a minimal CRISPR array) and maintain tight repression of cas1-cas2 expression in the donor cell, so that upon transfer they capture spacers from the chromosome and plasmids of new hosts and store them permanently in their own array. Subsequent PCR amplification and sequencing of these expanded arrays provide a molecular record of both the bacterial hosts and the co-resident plasmids encountered. We created SPI plasmids using the backbones of well-characterized mobilizable and conjugative plasmids RSF1010, RP4, F, and R100-1. We tested SPI plasmids in defined laboratory matings and in complex wastewater communities. The analysis of the acquired spacers successfully mapped permissive host ranges and profiled the co-resident plasmids in situ . Requiring only standard cloning, PCR and sequencing, this accessible and cost-effective strategy establishes a new framework for studying plasmid ecology. Because spacers are integrated chronologically, it further offers the potential to reconstruct multi-step transfer trajectories across natural microbial networks.

research.abstract: Abstract Amoeboid ochrophytes (stramenopiles) exhibit diverse cell forms and plastid states, yet many lineages are known primarily from environmental sequences. We describe Leucomyxa quisqueyensis sp. nov., a freshwater amoeboid ochrophyte isolated from a freshwater drainage channel in La Chinola, Santo Domingo Oeste, Dominican Republic. In established cultures, the isolate consistently formed extensive multinucleate reticula, with fine strands linking densely branched regions. The largest networks exceeded 2 mm. Confocal imaging revealed longitudinal microtubule strands along the reticulopodia. Rounded cysts measured 6.47–15.43 µm in diameter. SSU rRNA and nuclear phylogenomic analyses identified Leucomyxa plasmidifera as the closest sampled named relative. Their sister relationship received 100% ultrafast bootstrap support in the phylogeny inferred from 124 nuclear protein markers. The two species differed by 2.50% across comparable SSU rRNA positions and by 15.26% across 25,619 comparable amino-acid positions in the nuclear marker alignment. research.abstract: The Capsicum genus encompasses remarkable genetic and phenotypic diversity underlying its agricultural, economic, and cultural importance. Here, we present a Capsicum super-pangenome constructed from 48 chromosome-scale genomes, including 38 newly assembled, spanning all five domesticated taxa and their wild relatives. We identified 72,687 pangene families and abundant structural variants (SVs), revealing lineage-specific gene-content dynamics and patterns consistent with strong purifying selection against large SVs. A pan-NLRome revealed extensive presence-absence variation in the disease-resistance gene repertoire, with domesticated accessions harboring fewer NLRs than their wild progenitors. The graph-based super-pangenome enabled extensive genome-wide association mapping and robust genomic prediction across 130 agronomic and metabolic traits, leading to the identification and functional validation of RAP2 as a regulator of carotenoid accumulation and the discovery of a structurally complex terpene synthase locus associated with sesquiterpene ylangene. Pangenome-wide dissection of capsaicinoid biosynthesis further revealed evolutionary remodeling of the pathway through tandem gene duplication, interchromosomal rearrangement, and regulatory specialization. Collectively, our findings illuminate the genomic basis of Capsicum domestication and metabolic diversity and establish a comprehensive resource for genomics-assisted improvement of disease resistance, fruit quality, and flavor.

research.abstract: Streptococcus pyogenes causes diseases ranging from mild pharyngitis to life-threatening invasive infection, yet the genomic determinants of this variation remain poorly understood. We analyzed 1,863 publicly available genomes, whose pangenome comprises 6,568 genes (1,392 core and soft-core, 656 shell, and 4,520 cloud), and grouped isolates into 15 genetic groups with FastBAPS. Ten groups were monophyletic on the global phylogeny, and non-monophyly of the remaining five largely reflected the placement of isolates from group 12, which is dispersed across the tree. A GenomegaMap scan identified 163 of 3,147 genes with {omega} > 1. These genes were depleted among core genes and enriched among cloud genes, a pattern consistent with positive selection on recently acquired genes but also with the retention of slightly deleterious variation in young genes. A putative IS transposase (K07497) was the most consistent functional enrichment signal, which led us to analyze insertion sequence (IS) elements directly. In group 12, complete IS copies within genomes were more often near-identical than in other groups (OR = 1.46), consistent with more recent IS activity, and genes with {omega} > 1 were 2.9 times more likely than other accessory genes to lie within 5 kb of an IS element (8.8% vs. 3.0%; permutation p = 0.0006) after excluding IS-encoded genes. We did not detect this association in any other group, and most genes under selection were not IS-proximal.

research.abstract: Abstract Mutation rates are evolvable traits that respond to selection partly through the associations of modifier alleles with other variants affecting individual fitness. Yet, these variants can be subject to various selective regimes, whose respective role in shaping the evolution of mutation rates remains incompletely understood. To clarify the links between the fitness landscape and selection on mutation rates, we analyse a multi-locus continuum-of-alleles model where traits can affect both individual fitness and the mutation rates expressed across loci. We obtain a closed hierarchical system of moments describing the change in the distribution of traits, and thus in mutation rates, under small trait variation. We find that variation in mutation rates across individuals builds skew in the trait distribution, which plays a key role in the evolution of mutation rates; to track such asymmetries, we go beyond classical normal closure and adapt a cumulant-neglect method. We show that positive mutation rates are favoured by indirect selection out of evolutionary equilibrium (under directional, fluctuating or diversifying selection) and selected against at equilibrium (under homogenising selection). We illustrate these cases with a two-trait model, which we also study using individual-based simulations to evaluate the robustness of our deterministic results to genetic drift. Beyond these examples, our results classify the selective mechanisms acting on mutation rates and rank their importance according to the local shape of the fitness landscape and the variational properties of the population. This provides an account of the different ways selection can act on transmission fidelity in large populations. Article summary Selection can act on mutation rates indirectly, through its effect on new genetic variants. Here the authors built a mathematical model that summarises the selective mechanisms acting on mutation rates, given the shape of the fitness landscape. They show that higher mutation rates are favoured far from evolutionary equilibrium, under directional, fluctuating or diversifying selection, while lower rates are favoured near equilibrium, under stabilising selection. Individual-based simulations support these conclusions, and explore their limits in the presence of genetic drift. Overall the framework helps explain how selection regimes can shape the diversity of mutation rates across environments and genomic regions.
